utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated while you're waiting. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technicians, to the interpreters; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution. I think that we will have to hear the appearances. Madam Hollis, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Your Honour, Brenda Hollis, Kapila Waidyaratne, and Daniel Saxon appear for the Prosecution. In addition, I would like to introduce Susan Somers. Ms. Somers is a very experienced litigator within the Office of the Prosecutor who is replacing Michael Keegan, and in January or February, Ms. Somers will take over carriage of this case as the acting senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon is here as well, as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Defence, please. Let us begin with Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence is in the same composition. With me I have Mr. Branko Lukic, my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. There are no changes. Mrs. Jelena Nikolic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan and Zarko Nikolic are on the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. The Defence of the accused Radic is in the same composition: Toma Fila and Zoran Jovanovic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have Mr. Stojanovic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. There have been certain changes. We have a new co-counsel, Mr. Miodrag Deretic. He is a lawyer from Prijedor. I think that it will be interesting for me to mention that this is the first lawyer from Prijedor, and as we know very well, there are many cases tried before this Tribunal which occurred on the territory of Prijedor, so that I think that this innovation will assist the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of the accused Dragoljub Prcac is in the same composition, myself, Mr. Jovan Simic, and Mr. Dusan Masic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I should like to bid welcome to all new persons who have joined us both as members of the Defence team and the Prosecution team. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case. This is something that we should have done at the beginning but we can do it right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-98-30/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I think that we are now ready to proceed with our work. As you know, the parties were requested to prepare themselves for a discussion of a number of issues which are contained in the Scheduling Order, dated the 23rd of November, 2000. We are going to deal with these issues in the order that is indicated in the Scheduling Order. So we will first have a hearing for the arguments, since we have already received written submissions from the Defence and the response from the Prosecutor concerning the motion for a judgement of acquittal. We will hear all of those arguments together in the first part of the hearing, and then the second part of the hearing will be dedicated to a Status Conference with a view to prepare for the Defence case. I will first give the floor to the Defence counsel of Mr. Kos, since the Defence of the accused Kvocka has not filed a motion for judgement of acquittal. I will give the floor to the Defence counsel for Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may begin, Mr. O'Sullivan. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. For some reason, I'm getting the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you have made a lot of progress, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm hearing it but I'm not sure I'm understanding it. Good morning, Your Honours. As Your Honours know, on behalf of the accused Kos, we filed a motion for judgement of acquittal on the 6th of November. I will speak to that motion with two objectives: to clarify certain aspects of our motion and to respond to the Prosecution's filing of November 20, 2000. Let me briefly address Rule 98 bis. In our submission, the regime to be applied to a Rule 98 bis motion is determined by the Statute and Rules of the Tribunal and the precedents of this Tribunal. In regards to case law, we rely on two decisions which are referenced in our motion: the Kordic case decision of 6 April 2000 and the Kunarac decision of 3 July 2000. Both decisions interpret and apply the current version of Rule 98 bis. Can I briefly turn to the indictment. Your Honours will know that on the 13th of October of this year, a consolidated indictment was filed in this matter, which includes Schedules A to E. The schedules are part of the indictment pursuant to a decision of the previous Trial Chamber which had conduct of this matter, a decision of 12 April 1998. In that decision, the Chamber ordered the Prosecution to provide further particulars in regards to that indictment, and on May 31st, 1999, an amended indictment was filed with Schedules A through D which are now expanded to A through E. Those schedules specify charges against the accused. In our submission, where there is no evidence or insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction on one or more of the offences charged in the indictment, the Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal on that or those charges. Let me briefly address the charges alleged against Kos where we say there is no evidence. We say there is no evidence that Kos has any connection with the Keraterm or Trnopolje camps, or any individuals detained therein. There is no evidence that the following nine individuals listed in Schedule B were victims of persecution, inhumane acts, and outrages upon personal dignity. The nine individuals are: Refik Begulic, Mehmed Hadzic, Husein Hodzic, Senad Husic, Safet Ilic, Sakib Jakupovic, Besim Kodzic, Sakib Islamovic, and Ferid Mujcic. In addition, at paragraph 46 of the Prosecutor's response, the Prosecutor writes that: "The Prosecution accepts that there has apparently been no evidence admitted pertaining to these persons." Finally, under Counts 1 to 3, and by reference to Schedule B, there is no evidence linking Kos to alleged beatings and torture on Petrovdan. As requested in our motion of 6 November, this Trial Chamber should enter a judgement of acquittal in favour of Kos in relation to these aspects of the indictment. Let me briefly turn to where there is no evidence under Counts 4 and 5: murder. There is no evidence that the following six individuals were murdered by Kos. One individual in Schedule A is Izmet Hodzic. Four individuals listed in Schedule B are Becir Medjunjanin, Hanki Ramic, Mehmedalija Sarajlic, and Miroslav Soljaja. The one individual listed in Schedules C and E is Durat Dautovic. The Prosecution, in its response, made no response to our submission concerning these six individuals. We submit that a judgement of acquittal in favour of Kos should be entered in relation to these alleged murders. Those are the areas of the indictment where there is no evidence, Your Honours. I now turn to what we submit is an insufficiency of evidence. I'm referring to Witness AV, who testified before Your Honours. We submit that this witness did not tell the truth when he implicated Kos in alleged mistreatment. No other witness testified in relation to any alleged mistreatment by Kos against Witness AV. In other words, AV is the only person who gave evidence in relation to this matter. Can I briefly remind the Chamber of the testimony given by AV. The reference is page 5861 of the transcript. Witness AV was being questioned by Judge Wald. She asked him:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you ever see Krle present when a detainee was being abused or beaten in any of those places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, standing in front of them. I was made to slap other detainees, pursuant to his order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you are telling us now that there was a time when you saw when -- let me say, when he ordered you to slap somebody else? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, on re-cross-examination, following Judges' questions, Witness AV continued to insist on this version of events, which I note he had not spoken about prior to Judge Wald's question. And beginning on page 5863, Witness AV said that when Kos ordered him to slap someone that he simply had to do it with without objections. He said it was dramatic and traumatic for him. He said he would never forget it. But when confronted, Witness AV changed his story, and in our submission, he's been shown to be untruthful. He was asked in relation to his statement to the Prosecution:

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you never said that Krle ordered you to slap someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He never ordered you to slap anyone, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Witness AV is not worthy of belief, Your Honours. He lied to Judge Wald. He continued to attempt to embellish his story. He finally admitted Kos never ordered him to slap anyone. Witness AV was untruthful. His is the only evidence given in relation to alleged mistreatment by Kos of this individual. He can be given no credibility. His testimony should be ignored. Accordingly, we submit that a judgement of acquittal should be entered in relation to Kos in relation to this aspect of Counts 1 to 3. The final areas of insufficiency of evidence in our submission deals with three murders alleged against Kos. We say the evidence is insufficient to sustain the conviction of Kos for the alleged murder of the individual Crnalic. The only witness who gave evidence alleging that Kos shot and killed Crnalic was Witness AI. We say AI was unreliable and was mistaken when he testified that Kos was responsible. Can I remind Your Honours of this: AI testified that he believed Kos was not from Prijedor, the man he believed was Kos was not from Prijedor, based on his features and the way he spoke. Kos is from Prijedor. As we've shown in our written submissions, because of his physical state at the time, Witness AI's memory of events is unreliable. It's no small matter that Witness AI did not identify a guard named Drazenko Predojevic who he claims singled him out for this treatment. Why do we say this? The Prosecution knows who Predojevic is. He was indicted by the Prosecution. His photo was shown to the very next Prosecution witness, Witness B, who identified him. That's Exhibit 3/69B. We say the ability of this Witness AI to recollect people and events is quite unreliable. In addition, however, there are other reasons why we say Witness AI is unreliable. Two other Prosecution witnesses testified that someone other than Kos allegedly shot and killed Crnalic. Nusret Sivac testified that the guard who allegedly shot and killed Crnalic wore a hood and always manned a guard position between the "white house" and the pista. There's no proof that Kos ever held such a function. Second, Kermin Mesanovic testified that Kos was present at the time but Kos was sitting at a table, at the left corner near the "white house." There's no evidence that Kos had a gun or fired any shots. The second and third murders, and these are the final submissions on the insufficiency of evidence, relate to two alleged murders: Those of Abduhlah Puskar and Silvije Saric. Again, only one witness gave evidence in relation to that fact: Witness J. We say she is not credible or worthy of belief when she said that she heard Kos was present when these two men were beaten. Your Honours, there's no proof that she can identify Kos' voice; she did not identify Kos in court. We say that the evidence shows that Kos was not present in the camp when the alleged beatings occurred. And in her 1995 statement to the Prosecution, which she adopts as being voluntary and truthful, Witness J never stated that Kos was involved or present during the alleged beatings. I've spent some time talking about the issue of identification when we say the evidence is insufficient. We submit that the issue of identification is of significant relevance and importance under a Rule 98 bis motion, especially where the evidence of a witness is the only evidence given in relation to that fact. We rely on the Kordic and Kunarac decision in this regard. I've pointed out that in regard to Crnalic, Witness AI is the only witness whom we say is mistaken and unreliable, and what is more, two other witnesses testified that someone other than Kos allegedly shot Crnalic. In regard to Puskar and Sarajlic, similarly, only one witness gave evidence in relation to these events: Witness J. And as I've indicated, in her statement given five years ago, which she said provided the best recollection of all her experiences, which was made closer in time to the relevant events, she did not implicate Kos. Let me conclude by saying this, Your Honours: Rule 98 bis mandates that the Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal where the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on one or more offences charged. Each named individual and event we specify in our motion is a charge where the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction either because there's no evidence or the evidence is insufficient and unreliable. Both the Kordic and Kunarac decisions have held that where there is insufficient evidence, the accused is entitled to a ruling of no case to answer at this stage of the proceedings. We, therefore, respectfully request that you enter orders of acquittal, pursuant to Rule 98 bis, in favour of Milojica Kos as requested in the motion filed on his behalf on the 6th of November, 2000. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall be presenting the viewpoints for the accused Radic. The accused Radic has presented his views in the motion for judgement of acquittal for the accused Radic, and I shall repeat some of those elements contained in the motion in brief and will refer also briefly to the Prosecution response. I think that in this situation, and bearing in mind the response by the Prosecution, what is relevant and what we must talk about here is -- and we must look at Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute, because the counts in the indictment, if we take them in their order, 1 to 3 of the indictment, Counts 1 to 3, followed by Counts 4 and 5 and Count 8 to 9, must be viewed in the light of Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. At the outset, the role of the accused Mladjo Radic, his position in the Omarska camp, that is what I should like to talk about. The Defence is of the opinion and has presented evidence that the position -- as to the position of Mladjo Radic and the type of authority that he enjoyed in the camp. The Defence considers that the Prosecution has failed to present evidence which would indicate beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused Radic performed and wielded any kind of authority in Omarska camp. The evidence presented by the Prosecution are of such a nature that, in the best of cases, they can be evidence which is put forward indirectly. And we agree that Rule 98 bis provides for the fact that the Trial Chamber may, on the basis of presented evidence, bring in judgement and not that it should. And the Defence considers that with a respect for this standard which the Prosecution sets forth in his response by virtue of the evidence presented is of such a nature that they do not provide proof beyond all reasonable doubt as to the position and status of the accused Radic, as is represented in the indictment. And that is the first point, and we must start out from that assumption if his behaviour -- if he wished to express his behaviour following Article 7(3) of the Statute. From the evidence presented, we have not been able to ascertain beyond reasonable doubt that Mladjo Radic, within Article 7(1), directly performed criminal acts, and in the sense of Article 7(3), the evidence does not show that there was any command responsibility involved in his case. The Defence stressed that in his own testimony, the accused Radic indicated a certain kind of authority; but on the other hand, the Prosecution once again did not present evidence that it was the kind of authority which could prevent or punish the conduct of others, if he had knowledge of that kind of conduct and behaviour. There is no formal appointment for the indictment for Radic, and the Prosecution did not bring in any evidence to show formal appointment. Let me repeat what I have already said: That it is only indirect knowledge and the conclusions made by the individual detainees, or conclusions made generally that the accused Radic was in a position as guard -- head of the shift, but no formal evidence exists as we have seen it; and that the accused Radic in 1994 became the head of the shift within the frameworks of the Omarska police station. The Defence would now like to refer to the conditions that prevailed in the camp as a component part of the -- of persecution and inhumane conduct. No evidence has been provided that Mladjo Radic could, in general terms, with respect to the overall situation, change the conditions of detention at all, and here we include the hygiene conditions of the detainees, the food they received, and the water they were given to drink, and we have heard testimony and evidence about that at length. Sporadic attempts by the accused Radic to help and to see what could be done and to offer help or refuse to give assistance cannot indicate on sufficient grounds and evidence to indicate beyond any reasonable doubt that Mladjo Radic was in a position of that kind, that is to say, that he was able to change the conditions of detention for a large number of detainees or all the detainees. Let me repeat that it was only sporadic cases that we saw where the accused Radic did, in fact, assist. But these allegations of the witnesses of the Prosecution and Radic's own testimony do not indicate the possibility that he himself was generally able to alter the prevailing conditions in the camp. And I have already stated what conditions of detention imply and what the categories were that should have been changed, if that were possible. The Defence furthermore considers that insufficient evidence has been presented to show beyond reasonable doubt that Mladjo Radic could have changed the regime, that is to say, the rules that were applicable to detained persons in the sense of their freedom of movement, but also with respect to the arrival of their families or contact with them; and in that way, indirectly to have been able to change the conditions prevailing in the camp. Therefore, no evidence has been presented which would show beyond reasonable doubt that Mladjo Radic could have enabled detained persons to have contact with their families and in that way have changed the conditions of their confinement. The same applies to the application of the law of BH. Once again, no evidence has been presented which would indicate the possibility of somebody in the position as held by Mladjo Radic, the accused, could have applied those laws during the duration of the armed conflict, whose existence has been ascertained without a doubt. All the rules and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the day were derided, and as a policeman, that is to say, having the calling of a policeman - and there is official evidence, formal evidence to prove that, and no evidence was put forward to prove the contrary - Mladjo Radic was not in a position to apply any law whatsoever, except to implement the orders he received from his superiors. Briefly, those are the positions of the Defence of the accused Mladjo Radic presented in the motion for judgement of acquittal. Let me mention in this regard that as to Counts 14 to 17 of the indictment, we shall discuss these at greater length at another time. I have also touched upon the response by the Prosecution and should like to repeat that the Defence did take into consideration all the standards required by Rule 98 bis, and including the one that says that sufficient evidence is required for the Trial Chamber to be able to enter a judgement. And so in this phase of the proceedings, with respect to the accused Radic, the trial could be continued only with respect to Counts 14 to 17 of the indictment and not the rest. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Let us now hear the Defence of Mr. Zigic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall try and be brief. I usually do try. And in response to the Prosecution, I do not wish to repeat what has already stated in our written motion for judgement of acquittal. After the response by the Prosecution, we uphold everything we stated in the motion. It is our opinion that at this stage of the trial, the Prosecution nonetheless needs a standard beyond reasonable doubt to be applied to the case, because unless this standard -- if this standard is lacking at this stage of the proceedings, then the Defence has no need to answer the response, and it will not do so. And there will be no conditions for a sentence to be passed with regard to the accused and his incrimination. Having touched upon the question of standards, we are of the opinion that the standards for presenting evidence and proving guilt with this institution must not fall below the standards of the national laws both for war crimes and for ordinary crimes. Regardless of the atrocities that we have heard presented in this court, and I profoundly do believe that they did take place, of course, without entering into the realm of personal responsibility, I can never come to terms with the fact that, for example, that verbal abuse of one's neighbour, we would have to present far greater evidence than for a major war crime. Many details have been brought forward with respect to our own motion and the motion of the Prosecution. I should just like to highlight some of the elements in the Prosecution motion. For example, in paragraph 66 of the Prosecution response, it says that for the murder of a certain Spija Mesic, and this is something that Mr. Zigic is being accused of, it is sufficient to present the fact that one of the witnesses mentioned that that individual existed and that that individual was killed, was murdered; and on the other hand, that there was a constant and notorious presence of Zigic in Keraterm. That is not a sufficient standard. And let me mention, having said that, that we profoundly contest this term, the constant and notorious presence of Zigic in Keraterm. We contest that allegation. In our motion, we state that there is not a single piece of evidence to bear this -- to bear out the fact that Mr. Zigic killed Jasmin Izeiri or that this person Izeiri was in Keraterm at all. The Prosecution states that Witness Hase Icic says that Jasmin Izeiri died in Omarska. I think that the Prosecution, therefore, provides an argument to the advantage of the Defence, because the indictment states that Zigic killed him in Keraterm, whereas we now see that this person has died in Omarska. So the difference itself has overruled that charge. As a characteristic of this confrontation between Defence counsel and Prosecution, I should like to indicate paragraphs 78, 80, and 81 of the Prosecution's response where they make mention of the fact that the Defence of Mr. Zigic objected with regard to the form of the indictment. We should like to point out that this was the result of a misunderstanding, because we did not object to the form of the indictment at all. No objections were made there. Paragraph 78 relates to persecution. We do not claim that the indictment is lacking in form in that respect. What we are saying is that the evidence presented cannot lead us to conclude that Zigic can be charged for what he is charged in the indictment in that respect. Paragraph 80 of the Prosecution response relates to other inhumane acts, crimes against humanity, Article 5 of the Statute, and so on. We did not say that the indictment was lacking there. What we said was that the Prosecution has not provided a single piece of evidence and proof showing that those acts had been committed, or facts put forward which could come under that heading. Paragraph 81 of the Prosecution response refers to our standpoints with the application of Article 3 of the Statute. We did not actually say that there were any lackings in the form of the indictment, nor that there was an international conflict. That is an acknowledged fact. There was an international conflict and that is an adjudicated fact. But we consider that if -- that a state of war must exist to sustain conviction, and the Prosecution did not at any point state that a state of war actually existed. We cannot understand some other positions that have been taken, some legal constructions used in the Prosecution's response. To quote an example, I think it is paragraph 85 in that document, where it says that the Prosecution should maintain the fact that Zigic ordered certain detainees to perform fellatio although there is no evidence. So the Prosecution does acknowledge that there is no evidence to bear that out but that this should remain in the indictment. The same goes for the beating of Cirkic. The Prosecution maintains that this should be retained in the indictment, although not a single piece of evidence goes to show that. Now, we don't want to resort to the same kind of legal constructions. Our approach is very simple: Were these acts committed, and was there anything to prove -- any evidence to prove that they were committed? Another characteristic in the Prosecution's response has to do with the fact that we say that there is no evidence to show that Zigic beat up a certain Fikret Alic and Fahrudin Hrustic in Keraterm. In the response, it is stated -- that is to say, there is a combination of those names mentioned by two witnesses, that a certain Fikret Hrustic was beaten up, but, of course, those witnesses did not state that Mr. Zigic had any connection with that or that he was present when that occurred. The greatest problem, however, lies in the answers provided by the two witnesses that Fikret Hrustic was beaten up in Omarska, whereas in the indictment it states that this occurred in Keraterm. And there are many details of that kind. We don't want to enumerate them all at this point, but I would like to have the Prosecution supply us with the annex that is mentioned in paragraph 86. We did not receive the annex along with their response, but that is no hinderance for the Trial Chamber to continue working. I shall look at the annex later on, and I don't want to dwell on that. Having said that, I thank you for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. Let us hear the Defence of the accused Prcac. Mr. Jovan Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Dragoljub Prcac would like to point out, first of all, that in its written brief it has moved for a judgement of acquittal in respect of all charges against the accused and not in respect of separate acts and events, as the Prosecution tried to interpret it. I think that through the analysis of the evidence presented by the Prosecution, the Defence has shown that there is not enough evidence; that it has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Dragoljub Prcac is indeed guilty of the crimes with which he is charged in the indictment. At the outset, we should like to discuss the issue of the indictment itself. One has to ask oneself whether the indictment has to be a formal act or a kind of framework within which the Prosecution will move while presenting its evidence. The accused Dragoljub Prcac was charged with being the deputy of the commander of the Omarska camp during the period of time between the 24th of May and the 30th of August; was responsible for the acts with which he was charged in Counts 1 to 3, 4 to 5, and 8 to 10. If we should assume that the indictment is a formal act and that it is a basis for a fair trial, and the Defence must be notified of the charges against the accused, then in that case we should stick to this indictment during the presentation of evidence; that we should accept the fact, the requirement that the Prosecution had to present evidence to the effect that the accused was, indeed, in that capacity during the relevant period of time. I will support my submissions with a number of examples. But let me just mention at the beginning what happened here in these proceedings. We made an agreement at the beginning, after the arrest, that there would be a number of adjudicated facts, and we said that we would not be filing a motion on the form of the indictment but that we would try and agree on the form of the indictment. However, that did not happen, and the Prosecutor did not disclose to us all the necessary material in due time. If I remember correctly, in case of Witness K, the Defence wanted the testimony to be deleted because the witness in question never mentioned Mr. Prcac. We were never in possession of the material relating to Mr. Prcac, and we were not aware of the fact that the witness would testify against Mr. Prcac. But then the Prosecutor explained to us that it happened spontaneously. During the cross-examination that I conducted, and this is stated in the record, Witness K had spoken to the Prosecutor and had indeed mentioned Mr. Prcac, that she had indicated that she would be testifying against him; however, that piece of information was never supplied to us by the Prosecutor. At this point in time, the Prosecution is relying on the testimony of Witness K and trying to establish the credibility of the witness. The Defence does not wish to assess the credibility of the witness at this point; however, in order to take stock of the situation, in order to assess the facts, all of the witnesses must be properly assessed. The Defence has not skipped any single witness in their motion. We discussed every witness in our motion, but the Prosecutor failed to do the same. And let me illustrate this with a few examples, because I believe that by proceeding in this manner, one can end up with a completely false image of the factual situation. For example, it is stated that the accused Prcac was present during all shifts, and it is also stated that that was testified to by Witness Nusret Sivac. However, the record does not reflect that piece of evidence. I'm not going to enter into details regarding the testimony of the witness, but this information, as it is stated here, cannot be found in the record. He only mentioned that from time to time he would give the guards a list with names to read out. Further on it is stated that Mr. Prcac had a certain role in the camp, and then they support that with a number of witnesses and what they stated to that effect, and they claim that what the witnesses said was sufficient in order to support the allegation that Dragoljub Prcac was the deputy commander. Thirty-seven witnesses have been heard, and only two mentioned that fact. The Defence has offered an analysis of the command responsibility of Mr. Prcac in their written motion. The Prosecution had an opportunity to ask specific questions of all of its witnesses whether Mr. Prcac was there, what he did, and so on and so forth. But 17 witnesses failed to mention him, and the Defence maintains that those witnesses cannot be used as witnesses who proved that Dragoljub Prcac was in the camp during the relevant times. A number of witnesses didn't even recognise the accused, and there are a number of witnesses that talk about Mr. Prcac only in an indirect manner. There are 13 witnesses who have some -- who have provided some kind of information. Out of the 13 witnesses, we have shown, through our analysis, that seven witnesses had some kind of direct knowledge; five of them were women. So one has to ask oneself: What was the role of the accused, indeed? And was it possible for the Prosecutor to establish beyond any reasonable doubt that Mr. Prcac was the deputy commander. However, nobody saw him. He didn't walk around. And there were only a couple of sightings of the accused on specific locations within the camp. In their reply, the Prosecution is trying to revise their position. They say even if one should assume that Mr. Prcac was not the deputy commander in the camp, his mere presence would indicate a certain responsibility. We have had similar cases in this Tribunal, but in order to state that, one should prove that he was deputy commander and that he had certain authority. The Defence maintains that the Prosecutor has to prove that he was, indeed, the deputy of the commander; otherwise, they should indicate in the indictment that he had some other responsibility, some other kind of duty which enabled him to exert a certain authority in the camp. The second issue I wish to address is the relevant times. Mr. Prcac is charged with the offences for the period of time between the 24th of May and the 30th of August. Not a single witness for the Prosecution has testified about that. Not a single piece of evidence can be found to the effect that Mr. Prcac arrived in the camp before mid-July. All witnesses of the Prosecution who testified about the time when Mr. Prcac arrived in the camp claim that he arrived in late July, in mid-July, sometime between mid- and late July, at the very end of the existence of the camp. Not a single witness has claimed that he arrived in the camp before that. The Prosecutor is now saying that the time framework is not important. I don't know how to respond to this claim. I cannot even understand how one can have an indictment without the relevant times and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the relevant time framework. I don't know how we can discuss the importance of relevant times at all while discussing criminal offences and the presence of the accused in the camp. We believe that a person cannot be held responsible for something that happened before he was involved in the event. The Prosecution has not led evidence, either direct or indirect, to show that Mr. Prcac had had anything to do with the camp before or that he had had any functions, any duties, before, and that perhaps on the basis on those duties, those prior duties, that he would have exerted some kind of authority during the relevant times. They tried -- they attempt to say that during the indictment he had been an active policeman. Not a single witness has proved that fact. All of the witnesses of the Prosecution who have testified or who were cross-examined as to the issue whether Mr. Prcac was retired during the relevant times, they said that, yes, he was; their assumption was that he was retired. And there is not a single piece of evidence to the effect that he was an active policeman. If we adopt the criteria that the Prosecutor now wishes to establish, and that is that the mere presence of Mr. Prcac is enough here to sustain a conviction for what had happened in the Omarska camp and for what he was charged with in respect of the time when he was not there, and we know that we have an indictment which directly -- there had been an indictment which directly accused guards as perpetrators, but that indictment had been dropped. This Tribunal is supposed to try only the individuals who can be held accountable as commanders or those who can be held accountable as direct perpetrators. At one point in time, the Prosecutor tried to interpret its attachments to the indictment as only being of an illustrative nature. However, in paragraph 39 of the indictment, the Prosecutor states: "Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Milojica Kos, and Mladjo Radic instigated, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the torture and beatings of Muslim Croats and Muslim -- and Bosnian Croats, and they did so in search cases by direct participation in the acts which were described in the text and in annexes A and E." So in this paragraph, the Prosecutor is directly stating that there are charges for individual and for specific acts, and those specific acts were indicated in their attachments, in their schedules. The Defence has made an analysis of that material and claims with full responsibility that not a single piece of evidence concerning these individual acts show that those acts occurred during the time when Mr. Prcac was present in the camp. So these dates here, the dates that were indicated at the outset by the Prosecutor, could not be contested. Not a single murder out of six murders occurred during the period of time when Dragoljub Prcac was in the Omarska camp. They had occurred before that. And that is why it is very important for this Chamber to be informed of the fact that Dragoljub Prcac was in the camp between mid-July until the 6th of August, unless the Prosecutor can prove a higher hierarchial relationship. Inhumane acts and torture did not occur during the period of time when Mr. Prcac was in the camp. The analysis has been -- we have provided our analysis in our written brief and you have that in our motion. Can the Prosecutor then claim that Dragoljub Prcac, indeed, took part in the establishment of the camp since they haven't led any evidence to that effect? There is not, once again, a single piece of evidence to that effect. He arrived later on. He arrived at the time when the system was already functioning, when it was almost automatic. So we can perhaps ask what he was able to do later on, but only on the condition that he had certain authority. However, that authority, he didn't have it, according to the Defence. He was, as we have already indicated, a person who was involved in the administrative work. He was a kind of administrative assistant. And the witnesses have shown that, and I'm referring to the witnesses of the Prosecution. He never had the command responsibility nor was it ever proved during the Prosecution case that he had some kind of command responsibility. The Prosecutor is now trying to extend this concept of command responsibility. As regards the immediate perpetrators, the guards who were in the camp, the charges against them were dropped. I don't know on what basis one can retain the charges against Mr. Prcac if everybody who was -- if the charges against all of those who were at the same level as him were dropped. What do we have to prove that he was the deputy commander? Only the fact that one man left and the other one came instead. What the Defence would request of this Trial Chamber is that when making a decision, it attempts to view the statements of all the witnesses and not individual witnesses, as the Prosecution has done. A fair trial in the sense of Article 98 bis implies that all the evidence that has been presented be viewed and taken as a whole - taken as a whole. It is no good if just one witness is put forward, as the Prosecution has done, and to forget all the rest, to forget the 35 other witnesses, for example. And what the Defence wishes to raise as a question, an issue, here as well is whether, with evidence presented in the way that the Prosecution has done in the case of Dragoljub Prcac, what would happen if the Defence says that on the basis of this we don't want to present our case at this point, as it stands? Another fact that we should like to point out. The submission made by the Prosecution dealt with an assessment of the credibility of the witnesses. It is not the Defence that raised the question of credibility. We do not raise credibility in our motion and say that one witness ought to be believed and the other witness ought not. We just presented the facts before the Trial Chamber for them to -- for you to be able to ascertain whether anything definite can be determined and the charges that are placed against our accused. So of the seven witnesses, one witness said he was a deputy commander; another said that he was the main commander; one person said that he was a commander; one person said he was warden; the rest didn't know, and the rest are 32 witnesses in all. But together, taking what is in common to them all is that they saw him very rarely, that they don't know what his job is and what he did, and that he just carried those lists around. And the Prosecution is trying to manipulate those lists as well and says the following: "Mr. Prcac did call out the detainees, after which, according to the testimony of certain witnesses, those detainees were not seen anymore. They disappeared." That same statement from the same witness says in another portion: "Other guards called people out as well." It is not contested that on the 6th of August, when the detainees left for Trnopolje from Manjaca, it was not only Mr. Prcac who did the roll-call. A number of guards did the roll-call. And the Prosecution also wishes to manipulate the fact that he called out women when they went to Trnopolje on the 3rd of August and some of them later on disappeared. It is true that they disappeared and that we don't know of their whereabouts to the present day, but we don't know when they disappeared and we don't know whether Mr. Prcac was in the camp until the end; that is to say, we know that he was in the camp until the 6th of August. From the 6th to the 20th of August he was not there. These are the facts, the facts as they stand, the facts that must be looked into in all their complexity and their entirety. We do not have the right at this point to single out a fact, to single out a witness, and to interpret them falsely at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic [sic], I will take the opportunity of this little break to tell you that you will have to finish soon. You have four or five minutes, so that you can organise your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. My name is Simic. And having said what I said, I shall end there. So it is up to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was a misunderstanding. I don't think I said Stojanovic. I said Jovan Simic. I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am drawing to a close, Your Honour. This Trial Chamber would have to look at the facts completely, comprehensively, all-embracingly, and not individually, as best suits the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. I think we will now have a half-hour break, and after the break we will hear the response of the Prosecution. Our intention is to work until approximately 1.00 and continue in the afternoon in necessary. So if necessary, we will start in the afternoon at 2.00. So we will be working until 1.00, then we will have a one-hour break for lunch, and then we will resume at 2.00 if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Let us hear the Prosecution now. Madam Hollis, you have the floor for the response.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The arguments that you have heard today from the Defence are a summarisation of arguments that were made in their pleadings to which we have responded. So my comments will also be very summary in form and, I hope, very brief and very much to the point. The Prosecution suggests to Your Honours that the first issue that you must take on and you must determine is, first of all, what is the scope of the Rule under which you are acting. We suggest that many of the Defence arguments to you must fail because they are beyond the scope of the Rule, and it is the Rule which defines what actions you are entitled to take at this time. The scope of the Rule itself is very clear: Judgements of acquittal of offences charged, not material facts that are alleged in support of offences charged, not legal characterisations of the acts or omissions of the accused, and that is what you have under Article 7. Because if you look at the punitive articles, Articles 2, 3, and 5, the offence that is charged does not change based on the mode of liability or the legal characterisation of the acts or omissions of the accused. In Article 4, it appears that, indeed, the offence you would charge does change based on the mode of liability, so that you have genocide and then you have the possibility of conspiracy to commit genocide and then you have the possibility of attempted genocide and complicity in genocide. Those various charges, we suggest, in Article 4 reflect a real difference in the crime you charge based on how you legally characterise the acts or omissions of the accused. But the articles we are concerned with, Articles 3 and 5, that is not true. So Article 7(1) arguments do not follow within the scope of Rule 98 bis acquittals because you don't acquit them of Article 7(1) or Article 7(3), you acquit them of the offences that are charged. For that same reason, if you look at Rule 98 bis, you do not acquit someone of particular incidents that fall within the count, because it speaks about the offences charged. And if you look at what the offences are, they are the counts set out in the indictment, Counts 1 to 3. The counts are set out at page 10. And what are the counts? Persecutions, inhumane acts, outrages upon personal dignity. Those are the offences charged. And what is the general category of victims and the general time frame that is alleged? If you look at paragraph 24, it gives you the general parameters of the offences charged, and in paragraph 24, it tells you that they are charged, between the 24th of May and the 30th of August, with persecutions of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and other non-Serbs in the Prijedor area, based on political, racial, or religious grounds. So that is the parameter of the charge. And if you look at the other counts, you will find the same type of procedure followed. You have the count itself, which is murder, and then you have a paragraph that gives you the characterisation of the victims and the time period, and it is a very broad one. When we look at the schedules, the schedules are nothing more than further particulars that fall within the broad counts. And the question that you must answer is whether Rule 98 bis gives you the authority to enter acquittals related to specific incidents within a count. Because what offence will you acquit an accused of if you find that there is no evidence relating to one aspect, one incident, that is subsumed in the broader count. Is he then not guilty of Count 4, murder? Then you are ignoring all the other murders. So we suggest that you must first determine for yourself what is the scope of Rule 98, and we suggest that the scope is the offences charged and those are offences that allege cumulative acts, cumulative crimes, cumulative victims over a long period of time. So that Rule 98 does not envision entering judgements of acquittal for specific incidents within those counts. There is contrary authority in this Tribunal to that, and we have noted that, even as far back as Blaskic, which acted under the general authority that the Trial Chamber had, but also, I believe, felt that its actions were within the then new Rule 98 bis. They alluded to finding someone guilty of a part of an offence. We suggest, very simply, that that is beyond what is allowed by Rule 98 bis. Once you determine what is the scope of the Rule, then you must move to the remaining allegations made by the accused where you do have to look at the Rule and that they are within the scope of the Rule. What is the standard that you apply? We have set forth for you what we believe the standard is to be applied. We believe that standard is not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, that it is a lesser standard. And if we look for one brief moment at what is meant under the law by proof beyond reasonable doubt, of course what that means is that when you look at all of the evidence and you weigh the evidence and you judge credibility, that there can only be one explanation, one reasonable explanation for the evidence, and that is guilt. When you are faced with a Rule 98 bis motion, that is not the test you apply. Rather, it is: Is there some evidence which, if believed, would tend to reasonably establish each element of each offence. That is the test, and it is a lower test. Could you find the person guilty, not is there only one reasonable explanation which is proof beyond reasonable doubt. In applying the Rule 98 bis standard, we suggest again, as we have suggested in writing, that you do not look at the credibility issues, you resolve those at the end of the case; that you do not look at issues such as reliability unless you find that the only evidence that can support an element is totally unreliable, is totally incredible. Only in such a very limited circumstance at this part of the proceeding would you look at credibility or reliability. We also suggest that Rule 98 bis envisions some requirement on the part of the moving party to specify where the evidence is insufficient and to explain to you why, so that a general or broad assertion that the evidence is insufficient, the Prosecution submits, is not adequate basis for Rule 98 determinations and judgements of acquittal. If we look at the arguments that you have heard today, we find that many of the arguments go to the scope of Rule 98, and we suggest that perhaps the most clear example of where you must define the scope and act accordingly are those instances where we have admitted in writing that there appears to be no evidence of record to support individual murders. What do you do in that instance? If the scope of Rule 98 bis is such, as we suggest it is, that you must look at the crimes charged, that is, the broad murders, then you would not enter judgements of acquittal because there is no count upon which to enter a judgement of acquittal. If you determine otherwise, if you determine that you can enter acquittals for portions of a count, then your action would be different. But that is what clearly brings into focus -- that category of specific incidences -- what clearly brings into focus, perhaps your most difficult task, and that is determining what is the scope of Rule 98 bis. We suggest that when you have heard the Defence submissions this morning, and also in their written submissions, that they have mischaracterised the evidence. They suggest we have mischaracterised the evidence. Ultimately what the evidence is is determined by what is in the transcript or in a document, if that document is in question. You have been given references to the transcript, and we suggest that when you look at the language in those transcripts that it will support our position on the evidence. But ultimately, final determination must be made by Your Honours after you look at what is down in black and white, in writing, in the transcripts of this case. If you look at the arguments as well, and taking them now somewhat more individually, if you look at the arguments set forth on behalf of the accused Kos, it appears that one of their arguments is really an argument that is aimed against the Prosecution and not against the witness, and that is Witness AI, in regard to why we did not ask him to identify a photograph of Drazenko Predojevic. If they have an issue with the Prosecution, that doesn't impact this witness. Had this witness misidentified such an important person, we would have disclosed that to the Defence because it could have cast doubt on other identifications. No such misidentification occurred. Their argument about our failure to show him this photograph is, perhaps, an attack on us, but it says nothing of the reliability or credibility of this witness should you believe that that issue must be looked into. Regarding paragraph 10 of the submissions by accused Kos, where he talks about no evidence having been presented that Kos murdered Becir Medjunjanin, Mehmedalija Sarajlic, Hanki Ramic, or Miroslav Soljaja, we suggest that that is a general allegation that we do not have to address. We further suggest that there is evidence in the record of the murder of all of these victims, and we suggest that perhaps what is really being addressed here is that mode of liability can be limited at this stage of the proceedings, or a legal characterisation of the acts of the accused can be limited at this stage of the proceedings. Our position all along has been that we have charged the accused with particular offences and we have said that any mode of liability may apply, any legal characterisation of their acts may apply, under Article 7(1) or 7(3), and if any of those applies, their guilty. So that he does not have to have pulled the trigger or beaten to death any of these accused in order for you to ultimately, at the conclusion of these proceedings, determine he is guilty. There is some evidence of his position in the came; there is some evidence of his continuing presence in the camp; there is ample evidence of the conditions of the camp, of the open and notorious events that occurred in the camp, including killings, beatings, torture. We suggest that at least one mode of liability would support his being found guilty, even at the end of this case, of this murder, based on those types of evidence and that is the theory of common purpose which the Tadic Appellant Chamber set forth as a mode of liability under Article 7(1). In terms of whether a person testified to something or not, again, we have addressed that in our written submissions. We submit once again, very clearly, that at trial, Nusret Sivac testified to you that it was Krle's shift on duty when Crnalic was killed, and that the "testimony" that the accused Kos refers to is, in fact, questions about a prior statement and that Nusret Sivac disavowed the accuracy of that prior statement. Turning to the submissions by the accused Kos -- excuse me, accused Radic, we suggest again that a great deal of that submission goes back to the idea that Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) are offences charged; rather, they are modes of liability or legal characterisations. So that you cannot acquit a person of Article 7(1). You cannot acquit a person of Article 7(3). You can acquit a person of the counts that are set forth in the indictment. In regard to the distinction that the counsel made between indirect knowledge and conclusions versus formal evidence, we suggest that you can convict someone even if there is no paper anywhere which says that a person held a certain position. Rather, you can look to testimony based on observations and make that determination. Certainly, at this point of the proceedings, however, you look to see if there is some evidence which would support the accused's presence in the camp. The accused would allow you to legally characterise the accused's actions in any way under Article 7(1) or Article 7(3), and if you can find one mode of liability that is supported by the evidence, then we move forward and continue the case. Regarding the accused Zigic's presentations, we look at the comments regarding Izeiri. Again, we have noted that when there are disputes about the evidence, we look to the testimony of the witness, and in that regard, the Defence statement is correct in that in our written argument we had indicated that Hase Icic said that this man died in Omarska. Indeed, if you look at the transcript reference to which we have cited you, you will find that Hase Icic testified that a young Albanian man was taken out of Room 2 at Keraterm, so that the testimony of the witness relates to Room 2 at Keraterm, not Omarska. In regard to the comment that they did not receive the annex for their accused, annex 3 of the consolidated response to the motions for acquittal is the annex that relates to the accused Zigic. We filed that, and if they have not received that, we suggest that they ask the Registry for annex 3. If we look at the submissions by the accused Prcac, we again suggest that the test that is being applied is the incorrect test. It is not proof beyond reasonable doubt. There were comments made by counsel for accused Prcac that we were alleging mere presence was enough to support a denial of their motion for acquittal. Mere presence is not criminal liability. However, as was discussed in the Tadic case, there can be presence which is not mere presence. And we suggest there is some evidence of record to indicate that the presence of the accused Prcac was not mere presence but, in fact, was presence as part of an ongoing concentration camp regime of mistreatment of these victims, and that this presence goes far beyond mere presence and is one legal characterisation of his acts and omissions which could render him liable for the crimes in that camp. So we agree that mere presence is not enough. We suggest, however, in relation to Prcac, the evidence shows more than mere presence. Counsel for accused Prcac indicates, as one example, that we have stated that Nusret Sivac stated that Prcac was in the camp on all shifts and that he gave orders, and counsel indicates that the record does not show that. Again, we have given you references to Nusret Sivac's testimony. We would simply point you to page 4132, beginning at line 19, which is a question by Judge Riad who says:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, speaking of Prcac, you said that he would give orders to the guards. But did you also watch or notice that he was commanding one of the shifts? And the response is, beginning at line 24 of that page:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not a shift commander. He would be in all of the shifts. He would even come to the camp during the night very often, and he would bring lists with names of detainees with him. At page 4126 of the transcript, in response to a question by counsel for Mr. Prcac, at line 9:

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see Drago giving orders to someone? At line 10:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At line 11:

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To whom? At line 12:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the guards. Again, disputes about evidence in the record must be resolved by looking at the record. We have put our written submissions forward regarding the discussion of relevant times, and we suggest again that the relevant time is between the 24th of May and the 30th of August, and the crimes must fall within that time period, at whatever point within that time period they are covered by the offences. There was also reference to paragraph 39 of the indictment. We suggest that paragraph speaks to, again, legal characterisations or modes of liability and not to offences charged. In regard to this discussion of the schedules by many of these accused, if you look at the introductory section for all of these counts and all of these schedules, you will find it is a general reference; all prisoners in Omarska between these dates, all prisoners in Omarska and Keraterm for Zigic, all prisoners in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje for Zigic. So that each of these schedules incorporates this broad category of people and broad time in which these accused committed these crimes. We suggest that when you apply the proper scope for Rule 98 bis, when you apply the proper test, and when you look at how you apply that test to the evidence, that all of these challenges must fail. And we would ask you to proceed on all of the offences charged in the indictment. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. We will now give the floor to each of the counsel who wishes to intervene in order for them to reply, and you will all have five minutes. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have two points to make. The first is in regards to what my learned friend is describing as the scope of Rule 98 bis, and in my submission, the way in which that is tied to the indictment which includes the schedules. The schedules list specific individuals and events and allege liability of certain accused. Those lists, in our submission, are charges against the individual accused. My friend is quite correct that if you look, just as an example, to Schedule B for Kos - and I invite Your Honours to do that when you retire - there is a broad allegation of all prisoners, fixing a date, but that is followed by a list of seven names. Now, clearly the order of the previous Trial Chamber to set particulars must mean that the seven names which follow are made in allegation against Kos, and that's the way to read those schedules, in my submission, and that's the way to interpret and apply Rule 98 bis. And if there is no evidence or insufficient evidence, Your Honours must acquit. Can I also draw your attention to the Kunarac decision. Again, when you retire, I invite you to look at paragraph 26 of that decision, where, indeed, the Chamber entered a judgement of acquittal for a particular individual within a count because of an insufficiency of evidence. Your Honours will also see in that paragraph 26 that the Kunarac Chamber was applying the same test and standard as the Kordic Chamber. But I'll leave that with Your Honours to review. My second point is rather more specific and it is just what my learned friend said about the witness Nusret Sivac and the fact that his statement, previous statement, was read to him. Now, the first thing is that, as you know, only portions -- the relevant portions are read to a witness and that forms part of the record. That's part of his testimony; it is evidence. With all due respect to my learned friend, Nusret Sivac did not disavow his previous statement, he adopted it. He said it was truthful and voluntary and conducted over a considerable period. And what he said in evidence is that the person who allegedly shot Crnalic was not Milojica Kos. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan, and thank you for being so concise. Mr. Jovanovic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Article 1 of the Statute provides that the International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law, committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, in accordance with the provisions of the present Statute. Therefore, the sense and position of Radic with respect to the application of Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute is to be found -- is contained in persons responsible for serious violations, that is to say, Articles 2, 3, 4, and 5 of the Statute must be linked up, that is to say, they must be linked up with Articles 7(1) and 7(3), and the responsibility for a certain individual to commit criminal acts of that kind, that person must be in a position as stipulated by Article 7(1) or 7(3) of the Statute for us to be able to apply the other articles linked up with Article 7(1) and 7(3), which provide for criminal acts as quoted. Therefore, criminal acts, the ones in the indictment and the counts in the indictment and the crimes committed, cannot exist independently of Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute, unless we determine the position of the accused in the sense of these two articles of the Statute. Then one element will be lacking in the criminal act or criminal acts which the accused is being charged of on the basis of the indictment. And it is along those lines that the Defence said that the evidence presented does not indicate the position held by the accused Radic. So one vital element is lacking in that chain. The same is true with respect to the conditions that prevailed in the camp. The status, once again, of the accused Radic has not been determined or ascertained, and the possibilities he had to influence those conditions and ultimately to change them. So much from me, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just two or three very brief remarks. We do not see any basis for this Trial Chamber to burden itself with certain events for which no evidence has been presented. It is a very complex and very expensive case, very expensive proceedings, indeed, and I think it would be of great assistance to all of us to simply stop discussing the events for which no single shred of evidence has been presented. This remark concerns the allegation of the Prosecutor that the partial acquittal of certain counts in this stage of the proceedings is unacceptable, if I have correctly understood the position of the Prosecutor in that respect. I think that that kind of argumentation would lead to the conclusion that the Chamber would not be in a position to do so at the very end; that is, it could not bring a judgement of that kind, so the accused must be acquitted of certain individual counts. Therefore, I believe that this argument cannot be accepted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic is next. I think that I have pronounced your name properly and stated it properly. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would, first of all, like to remind the Trial Chamber of the fact that the Chamber, practically in the identical composition, made a decision in the Jelisic case, and I do not think that the criteria -- that that criteria is the criteria that has to be applied here and now today. With respect to Mr. Nusret Sivac, the Defence would like to state that it is impermissible that we draw parts out of context, because if you extract parts and portions out of context of the whole testimony, you have a half-truth, and half-truths, in the respectful submission of the Defence, is worse than a complete falsehood. Nusret Sivac said that Mr. Prcac was present during all the shifts. That means that he was present during all the shifts that took their order one for another, and the Prosecution said that he attended the shift change, which means that they are alluding to the fact that he was present, that he was in charge of the takeover of shifts, and that on the basis of that he had an authority of some kind. No. What the witness said was that he was present during the shifts. The witness also said that he does not know what he did. He saw him with some lists in his hands, that sometimes he would give the guards those lists to read, and that was the end of his testimony. The witness never said that he was present and attended the actual changeover of the guards at their shifts. So they are using a half-truth. What the witness said was that he was there and present in the space of 24 hours when the shifts were on duty, but no authority during the actual changeover and takeover of the shifts. That is what I wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. I think that my colleagues have questions for you. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Good morning, Ms. Hollis. I have a question of a general character, without going into the merits of the motions, and concerning exactly your view and concept concerning the scope, the scope of the Rule 98 bis. In essence, you consider that 98 bis only envisions a conviction on a charge and not a portion of a charge, or an instant. Now, I just want to be enlightened and to know more. I want you to develop this view more in the light of several considerations. The first is another, more or less, general rule which I know in French, I don't know in English, which says, "Qui peut le plus peut le moins." If you can do more, you can do less. So if we can acquit on a charge, we can acquit on a portion of a charge. Now, in that case, is this in the interests of the Defence or not? And is that -- does this put the Prosecution into any disadvantage? And would this be in the interests of the Court or not? The first question: Would this put you into any disadvantage? And then would it be of any benefit to the Defence? It would alleviate their burden. And of course the accused is entitled to have any alleviation of burden. It could be economical; it could be expedient. So in light of these considerations, why would you consider that Rule 98 bis only envisions charges and not a portion of a charge? Thank you so much. And I just want a small question for Mr. Simic, also without going into any merits. You mentioned that Mr. Prcac would only be reading lists, and I think I put this in connection with what you said that he had an administrative role. Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So reading lists for people to be -- whatever done with them is only administrative. It's not an order. He's a clerk, he's just like a clerk. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He read out lists not as he saw fit but pursuant to orders. He had the same status and was at the same level as all the other guards. Nothing more. Someone stood guard; other people dealt with the radio; and he was in -- he read lists. From time to time he read these lists when he wasn't on duty by the radio station, the radio transmitter. So this was ordered by Zeljko Meakic and so forth, and there is sufficient evidence to bear that out in the testimony of the witnesses. In addition to that, Your Honours, there is evidence that other guards read lists too. This occurred on the 6th of August. There is testimony that it occurred on the 3rd of August as well when the women were transferred to Trnopolje. And we heard testimony that other guards called people out as well, not at the very end of the camp, when the camp came to an end, but during its duration. This wasn't his exclusive duty, it was just one of the jobs that he did as a guard in the camp or, rather, as an administrative worker, clerk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Reading the list, knowing what this would entail, do you still consider that this is only an administrative, clerical function?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me remind you, if I may, of part of the testimony when my learned colleague, Mr. Saxon, was examining Witness U, and he said the following: "Dragoljub Prcac determined which women would stay on in the camp," of the names he read out, "and which ones were to be transferred to Trnopolje." And the witness said, no, he just read out the names. There is no evidence to support that he had any authority in any way whatsoever. He was just noted because one of his duties was, at one point, to read out a list. He didn't know why he was doing this; he didn't know what was on the lists. And then we have the testimony of Omer Mesan, and the Prosecution erroneously interpreted what that witness said. They read out the lists of witnesses, and on that occasion, Dragoljub Prcac and some unidentified guards said that there were 50 detainees more than were on the list, which indicates the fact that they didn't know how many detainees there were, where they were supposed to go, and the kind of behaviour exerted towards them. All they did was read out what they had. And Omer Mesan said that. But the Prosecution made this appear as if he determined where they were to go. All he did was to read. That was just one of the jobs that he was assigned to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish to reply, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Either now or when my colleagues have finished their questions. It's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If Your Honours would permit, it would be easier if I would answer it now or answer them now. Your Honour, in regard to the adage that if you can do more, you can do less, we suggest that that depends upon the language or the intent of the statutory provision or Rule that you were implementing. For example, if you are looking at sentencing, and it says that the maximum imposable punishment is imprisonment for the person's natural life, that means you can do less. But if you are looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Ms. Hollis. It is difficult when counsel speaks amongst themselves because we can pick up your voices via the microphone. Your voices are registered via the microphone. So I apologise, but would you please pay attention to that and please refrain from speaking amongst yourselves. Ms. Hollis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So we suggest that no, you cannot always do less if you can do more, and it depends upon the Rule or the statutory provision. When we look at Rule 98 bis, we suggest that it is a Rule which is limited in its scope because what it is doing is it is stopping mid-trial, before the Defence puts on any evidence, and it is prematurely, if you will, entering a judgement. So for that reason we suggest that it is limited in its scope. And we further suggest that the plain language of the Rule limits its scope. It could have said that you can acquit on all or part of a count. It did not say so. It said an offence. And we suggest that because it is a Rule which does not favour a broad definition but rather favours a narrow definition, because in fact it is interposing a judgement at the mid-point of a trial so that you narrow the scope of what you do rather than enlarge it. That would be our response to the adage that you quoted. In regard as to whether it is in the interest of the Defence, we suggest that on a very broad and philosophical level it would be in the interest of the Defence any time you would drop out a particular incident. If you were to use that argument, then you could look at all the material facts that are alleged in an indictment and you could at mid-trial sift them out. Would that somehow benefit the Defence? In a very broad way we say it would. Does it benefit the Defence in the sense that it gives them an acquittal of the count that is actually charged? No it does not. So it doesn't benefit them in that way. Does it benefit us or is it harmful to us? That's hard to say, Your Honour. What would happen if, during the Defence case, one of their own witnesses would come out with proof of the killing of one of these victims? In the normal course of events, if you went forward with the charge and the offence, you could consider that evidence in your final decision. If you acquit on that specific victim at mid-trial, then, of course, we would suggest that you wouldn't be able to do that. So in that sense, we think it's probably unlikely that it would happen, but in that sense, it would be of some detriment to the Prosecution, and in broader terms, a detriment to a final determination in accord with what actually happened at these camps and what is charged as having happened. Would it be economically expedient? Would it be judicial economy? Well, Your Honours, we have closed our case in chief, so the evidence is as the evidence is. I don't see the judicial economy of entering judgements at this point on something that is already in the record or not in the record. So I don't think it would speed up your process; I don't think it would slow down your process. So those would be my general submissions, Your Honour, to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I just add an explanation of my question, because to take your test, your criterion, you said that there should be no evidence reasonably established to sustain a conviction. This would be the criterion to acquit. Now, the fact, as you said, that the Prosecution has finished its part and its evidence which means they have no more evidence to prove, and in the light of what the Prosecution -- this is just for the sake of understanding -- and there is no chance to get more proof of a certain incident or a part of a crime or one of the -- let's say one of the instants, we don't expect any more proof. And in light of what the Prosecution has offered, there is no reasonable chance of conviction. Now, if we -- if the Chamber deals with this, wouldn't that dispense, alleviate, the charge of the Defence in the sense that they do not need to bring witnesses to disprove this fact which is already -- which is already out of the trial, because there is no reasonable -- there is no reasonable evidence for it, and it is just making it clear that there are certain things which don't require any more waste of time and waste of money for all the Tribunal. That was the issue. Of course, if you consider that this will disturb the totality of the trial, that's another thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
