utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, the accused have no burden at all to disprove or prove anything. So that if there is no evidence now about these specific incidents, they certainly have no burden to even deal with these instances. So it doesn't impose a burden on the Defence, and, in fact, the Defence has never had a burden and does not in a criminal trial have a burden of any sort. They may choose to put on a case, not because they have a burden but because they choose to. So no, it doesn't alleviate a burden because no burden exists. If we could perhaps just focus the real heart of the issue, if I may be allowed to, the Prosecution's position is this: If we had charged these accused with a specific count of murder for each named victim, if we had done that, at this point in the proceeding, within the scope of Rule 98 bis, Your Honours would enter judgements of acquittal relating to those specific victims that are individually charged and victims for which we have no evidence. So if it were a count, you would at this point within the scope of the Rule, we submit, enter a judgement of acquittal. So it does come back to, again, the scope of the Rule, and we have discussed our position on that. Our position is you -- there's nothing to enter a judgement of acquittal on because the count is a cumulative count and includes many victims. So you can't find them not guilty of the count. And because we have not individually charged those individual murders, there's no count to find them not guilty of. But that is what Your Honours must decide in your determination of what the scope of the Rule is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you again, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the court reporter for English is having a problem. Have you got a replacement?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may take a break, a short break. May we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My questions are for Ms. Hollis. The first one is somewhat of a follow-up to Judge Riad's, because I think it is a difficult barrier that you're trying to surmount here, and the theory, I know, is -- I understand the charge is murder and there are some incidents which are cited in the schedule; however, I'm always drawn back to the fact that the original Chamber which had this said that you had to provide those schedules in order to give the Defence some opportunity to prepare for the trial. I mean, in other words, you couldn't have gone and just said: "You're guilty of murder under Article 3 and under Article 5." It simply wouldn't have -- it wouldn't have withstood any kind of, I think, of a motion to dismiss unless you had these annexes. And now at the end of the period where you have some of these incidents or specific instances which you have no evidence, you say, "Just keep them in there until the end. Maybe something will show up in the Defence's case which will make our case for us." But if I were a Defence counsel, I wouldn't be too comforted by that. I guess I would feel that as long as those incidents were in the indictment and hadn't been dismissed by the Court after a motion for acquittal, I'd better prepare for the defence to some degree. Why doesn't it make sense to get rid of the brush -- the underbrush, and as we move into the second part of the case, focus on those incidents in which you did have enough evidence to withstand a motion for acquittal? Why carry this dead weight just on the chance that maybe something will show up in the second part of the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think that it goes back to the fundamental issue that Your Honours face, and that is, what is the scope of Rule 98 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I will give you time. My point is: Like Alice in Wonderland, I think that, you know, there are words there and it's up to us to interpret them. I don't happen to read 98 bis as saying under no circumstances can you ever dismiss one of the incidents or -- and, indeed, two other Trial Chambers, as you have suggested, have gone that way. So I don't know that it's a clear statement. I think it's more a question of our interpreting in a way that makes sense both for justice and for the procedure of the trial. Go ahead. I'll let you finish now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I do think that since it is a Rule that we suggest is a Rule that is limited because it is this decision at mid-term in the trial, that it is a Rule which needs to be read by the plain language of the Rule, and certainly as regards other Rules, this Trial Chamber itself has made that determination, that you must strictly interpret the Rules, such as the Rule for affidavits. So we suggest that the Rule does say offence or offences charged, and that's what it means. And when you come to the order of the Trial Chamber, it was basically in the form, we suggest, of a bill of particulars, to give further specific -- and we suggest they are material facts in support of the count which is the cumulative charge of murder of many --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- so we believe that it does not transform those into individual counts of murders. If it does, we would very much like to know that interpretation because it will influence how he approach sentencing should we get to sentencing. But we believe that does not transform that into individual counts, and if it does not, we believe that the Rule, by its language, does constrain the entering of judgements of acquittal. We again suggest there's really no further work to be done in regard to individual incidents, so that it is not a burden to either the accused or the Chamber, because the accused have looked at these. We have said there is no evidence on these specific incidents, so they have no reason to delve into the incidents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So yours is a pure Rule interpretation argument, because contrary-wise, there's no burden to you if we say -- I'm just using this as an example here. If we say the seven or the six, whatever it is, murders that Kos says that you admit there was no evidence on, and we say, "Sorry, those go out," we haven't thrown away the murder count. I mean, you still have your murder count, you still have your Article 3 count and Article 5 count. So you haven't suffered anything except the possibility that something might come up later in the case. So, I mean, it has to come down to your argument that we don't have the authority under that Rule to do what two other Chambers have already done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, we do. We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And we do suggest that it is very unlikely that evidence would come out through the Defence case of these victims. But if it does, these are very serious offences -- incidents within a very serious offence, and then what would the Chamber do with that evidence? And it would not necessarily be evidence that we would try to bring out. So we again go back to what are the counts, what are the offences charged, in the scope of Rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So, then, how would you sustain your burden of proof under that scenario? Because if you admit at this point -- in our case in chief we put on nothing, and then a Defence witness gets on the stand and blurts out something which does not -- not as your witnesses but as one of the Defence witnesses, have you sustained your burden of proof?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If he gives you evidence that convinces you beyond a reasonable doubt that this incident also should be included, then, yes, we have. You are not limited in the Defence case to using it for the Defence's benefit or using it purely to contradict Prosecution evidence. Whatever comes out in the Defence case, you may use in making your final decision in this case. So we believe, yes, indeed, it would depend on what that person said in their testimony, but that could be the basis for you to include another incident within the overall count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. I have a second line of questioning, and that is that on several -- you have told us that you don't think we should consider any particular theory of liability at this juncture, that that would come later; that "any mode of liability that could conceivably result in finding guilt, we have to consider." But I have to say that it does seem to me that if we are considering whether or not there is a sufficient amount of evidence that a reasonable Chamber could find the person guilty or could not, that has to be tied to the theory of liability. And let me tell you what I'm saying. For instance, you've used reference both in your written materials and here many times to the so-called common purpose theory. I have to tell you, I'm not sure what you mean by the common purpose theory. There's one paragraph or two paragraphs in Tadic which were not applied in that case. Common purpose theory, to my knowledge, has never been applied -- except for a few lines of Kupreskic, but that's a completely different situation. It's never been applied, to my knowledge, in a concentration camp case. Therefore, it's not particularly helpful to me for you to say, "Well, Mr. Prcac, he might be found liable under common purpose theory," and then you just tell us mere presence isn't enough, but presence plus notoriety of the conditions plus status. I don't know what if any authority you have to say that even if that were so, Mr. Prcac, you could go backward and say that he was liable for things that happened before he even got to the camp or maybe you don't say that but I don't know whether you said that or not. Or even more perplexing to me, that any of these people, with the exception of Zigic, who is alleged specific instances which took place at Keraterm and Trnopolje, the rest -- I looked over your own annex, I can't find a word connecting them with the other two. So I don't have any notion of what you think common purpose is. Does it cover the three camps? Does it go backward on liability to May 24th before Prcac even came to the camp? And I'm wondering how, therefore, I'm supposed to try to assess whether or not there's sufficiency of evidence. I think at some point this has got to be cleared up. I mean, I know the theory, I've read the Nuremberg cases, but they don't explain it with any detail either. So it's not like a magic wand you wave around and you say "common purpose," and you've invoked the Holy Grail. I don't know what you mean by common purpose. I don't expect you to give me the full explanation, but I'm pointing out to you a problem I'm having in making that determination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that to my attention, Your Honour. In this Tribunal, the Tadic Appellant Chamber dealt at length with common purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: A couple of pages of dicta basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If you would look at the Appellate decision, beginning where they begin to talk about modes of liability, really, under paragraph 185 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- but when you begin with 195, where it says: "Close scrutiny of the relevant case law shows that broadly --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I apologise. "... the notion of common purpose encompasses three distinct categories of collective criminality," and that goes all the way through paragraph 228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have read the whole thing, but I don't think it answers some of the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It does talk about concentration camp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- common purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, right. But it says that's one of the three instances of common purpose --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- but it really doesn't answer any of the questions that we would have to answer here, or that I would have to answer, to know whether or not if we use the common purpose theory, Mr. Prcac or maybe some of the others too would be liable for what? What would be the scope of their liability under --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It goes back to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but both of you are speaking the same language, and I think that our interpreters have problems following you because there were no pauses between questions and answers. We've been telling this to the Defence counsel, but please bear this in mind, the necessity of making a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And I as well, Your Honour. You have certainly asked me to keep that in mind before. I do apologise. I would suggest, Your Honour, that the Appellate decision does give you what you need because it gives you the elements, it gives you the theory; and what we suggest to you is that when you're looking at what happened in the other camps, that is the context in which these individual acts of the accused must be considered, because it does give you the broader common purpose, if you will, the common enterprise, of what was happening in opstina Prijedor. It is related to the findings that this Chamber has previously made, and that is that the mistreatment of persons in these camps was connected to the widespread or systematic attack and the armed conflict. It is within that context and using that as evidence to show some of the elements required for these offences that you will ultimately, as a Trial Chamber and as individual Judges, have to legally characterise what these accused have done. So, for example, Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- taking your example of what happened in Omarska before the accused Prcac arrived, can you find him guilty under common purpose of the actions that occurred before he acted at the camp? We suggest you may very well find you cannot. However, what happened prior to his arrival and happened during his stay is proof of the regime of the camp which does go to common purpose. So we believe that would have significance for you. And our point about modes of liability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How about -- if you wouldn't mind addressing what is really bothering me: Keraterm and Trnopolje. Are you really suggesting the common purpose; that if they joined up, as it were, in Omarska, they are going to be held responsible for what happened at Trnopolje and Keraterm? Not defendant Zigic but the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What we are saying is that in showing the breadth of this common purpose, we are using these other camps. It was connected in this broader common purpose. In legally characterising the import of the accused's conduct at Omarska, we believe that the conduct of what was happening in the other camps is relevant. As to whether you are going to say they are liable for what happened in those other camps, we are not saying you may necessarily do that. What we are saying is it is a relevant context in which to ultimately determine what mode of liability, if any, you may apply to their acts or omissions, because ultimately, of course, it is their acts or omissions that you're looking at for liability. But in determining the scope of that liability, and looking at the Common Purpose Doctrine, there is even a third category that says you didn't specifically intend the result in a particular place but it was reasonably foreseeable in the common purpose to which you became a part. So that is something for final determination as to exactly how broad that goes. But certainly for purposes now, we believe it is a relevant context in which to determine if there is any mode of liability on which there is some evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand your basic -- and I would agree with your basic notion -- pause. I would agree with your basic notion about looking at any possible mode of liability. I think you understand from your answer what my problem is, that nobody -- I did not find the Tadic dicta sufficient for me to determine what you were talking about as the common purpose mode of liability that would be applied here. I assume at some point in this whole proceeding you'll brief that a little bit more down the line. But what you have said has helped me to some degree, so thank you. End of pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I didn't address your question. Perhaps I'm too obtuse, but I intended to address it. I apologise if I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Madam Hollis. In follow-up to the issue that has just been discussed, I should like to ask a question and hear your views about certain doubts that I have at the moment. And I hope that you will help me clarify certain things. You'll remember that this case was, at the very beginning, Radic, Kvocka, Zigic, and Kos, that it involved four accused; however, Zigic was made part of this case because of his involvement in the events in the Omarska camp. But he was also the accused in one other case, Simic, I think, involving the events that took place in Keraterm and Trnopolje. At one point in time, the Zigic case was joined to the present case, so he was accused for the events that took place in Omarska, and in addition to that, he was joined in the sense that he participated in the events that took place in Keraterm and Trnopolje. Am I correct, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question in relation to that is the following: Before Zigic was joined with this case, including the Trnopolje and Keraterm events, the other accused at the time, Kvocka, Kos, and Radic, were already held responsible, according to the theory of the Prosecutor, for the events that took place in Keraterm and Trnopolje, or not. Was that the case? Were they held responsible for those events as well, before Zigic came to this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we exclude Zigic from discussion, the events in Trnopolje and Keraterm are relevant to the charges against these accused because it is part of the broader crime that occurred in Prijedor; it is part of the ethnic cleansing of the municipality of non-Serbs. So in that regard, the context is significant. The context is also significant because the evidence of those camps further supports that there was a regime within the opstina Prijedor of repressive conduct toward non-Serbs in camps. So it is significant for that as well. Why is it significant? It is significant for the common or jurisdictional elements; it is also significant for intent and inferring intent; it is also significant for different legal characterisations of the conduct of these accused, different modes of liability, if you will. That's where we go back in to proof, first of all, that there was this common purpose; to proof that it could extend to this concentration camp regime, so it was relevant to all of that. If we look at the counts themselves, as we talked about earlier, and if we look at persecutions, for example, we look at what was actually stated in there and we look at, for example, paragraph 24 - paragraph 24 in the indictment basically indicates that they were guilty of persecutions of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and other non-Serbs in the Prijedor area on political, racial, and religious grounds - now, if you look at that language, it does not say they're guilty for what happened in Keraterm or they're guilty for what happened in Trnopolje. We suggest that at the conclusion of this case, when Your Honours decide the parameters of their liability, if any, under common purpose, that it is possible that Your Honours could determine that they are guilty of crimes in those other camps because they took part in a common enterprise. The intended result for them was to continue the regime in Omarska, or it was to inflict the specific types of abuses that are alleged, or -- and you can either argue that they also intended for the other abuse, so that they are guilty under this common purpose theory, or you could find that they limited their intention to what happened in Omarska, but they were aware that the regime of misconduct would reasonably include the same type of crimes at Keraterm and Trnopolje. Under the third theory of common purpose, if you are a part of the common purpose and you don't intend a specific result but that specific result is reasonably foreseeable based on what you do intend, then you can be found criminally liable for that as well. So when Your Honours conduct your ultimate deliberations, you may conclude that they were liable for these other acts of misconduct. And then the question would be, really, the degree of liability. And if at some point causation does break off, and that even if you find they were liable because it wasn't in the camp in which they were working, then on sentencing you would reflect that with a lesser sentence. But we believe that is a permissible final determination you could make, and it is encompassed within this theory of common purpose, which is one mode of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Ms. Hollis, in view of what you have just told us, can I conclude that in the Simic case, the accused in the Simic case are also responsible for everything that we are discussing here concerning the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think this is an issue as to when does liability attach. Yes, Your Honour. And that is something also that Judge Wald had raised as a problem for her and a question for her. We suggest that the issue is one for resolution at the conclusion of the case because of the way the counts are alleged, but we would suggest to you this: that the determining factor would be, we would suggest, when the person joins the common purpose. So that even if an accused came to the camp at, say, the end of July, which is not the case here, but the end of July, if they had joined the common purpose earlier and if Your Honours could determine that what happened in these camps was reasonably foreseeable given the common purpose they had joined, then, yes, they could be held guilty for what occurred in these camps prior to their arrival at the camp. So we suggest the real legal issue, and it's not a legal issue for discussion under judgements for acquittal, we suggest, but the legal issue is when does the evidence show, either directly or through reasonable inferences, that the person joined the common purpose, that they became a part of it? And that is the point at which liability would attach. The evidence of what happened before that would still be relevant to Your Honours because it does establish the ongoing nature of the enterprise; it establishes what the common purpose was. Because individuals don't all have to be present at the creation of the common purpose, they can join later. That's the fatal flaw with the argument put forth by the counsel for the accused Prcac. You don't have to be in at the beginning. Any time you jump on board, your liability commences. So when they would be liable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the transcript anymore. There seems to have been a problem. I was trying to have a break but I don't know now. I think we should have a break before our Status Conference. Madam Hollis, could you perhaps just finish your intervention, and then we will have the break, because we're not getting the transcript. Yes? No, nothing is being written down at the moment, because we don't have the court reporter in the courtroom here. I think that the best way would be to have a break at this point, and we will come back to finish your argument, Ms. Hollis, and to begin the Status Conference. So a one-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Ms. Hollis, as you can see on the transcript, the last sentence that you uttered was "they don't have to be in at the beginning." Please continue with your argument, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have reviewed the last part of the transcript, and the part I reviewed also had the sentence "They can join." I have also recalled the principle or adage that Judge Riad has set forth: If you can do more, then you can do less. We have argued that that principle does not apply to Rule 98 bis. However, that principle would apply to my comments, Your Honours, and I have nothing further to say unless you have additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have one more question, Ms. Hollis. What I wanted to know was whether in the Simic case the accused will also be held responsible for these actions that were committed in the Omarska camp. But let me, perhaps, try to rephrase the question. Before the joinder in the Omarska case, the acts for which Zigic was held responsible and which took place in Keraterm and Trnopolje, did the configuration of the indictment, if I can put it that way, did it change? So before Zigic was joined to the indictment, did the accused that were already present there in Omarska, were they accused for the acts committed in Omarska as well, or did that happen only at the moment when Zigic joined them with the acts that he committed in Keraterm and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I think, to clearly answer that, we have to look at the counts themselves and the language of the counts. If we look at the murders, I believe, in regard to the four accused -- or the three accused who were in the case before Zigic, the murders talked about prisoners in Omarska. If we talked about the torture counts, I believe that those counts in the relevant paragraph referred to prisoners in Omarska. When we looked at persecution, I believe I earlier alluded to that language, and that language was in the area of Prijedor, so that that was broader. Given that, Your Honours, we would suggest the following: For Counts 1 to 3 for Kvocka, for Radic, for Kos, and later for Prcac, that it is possible that Your Honours could, on the language of the indictment, find them guilty for what happened in those other camps using one of the modes of liability that is referred to as common purpose, and that is the third mode of liability that says that you join a common purpose intending certain things. Other crimes occur which were not within the intent that you had but they were reasonably foreseeable. Under that mode of liability, you could conclude, we suggest, they were liable for crimes in Keraterm and Trnopolje. The language of the indictment would allow you to do that. We suggest further that is a decision for final judgement. That is not a decision for Rule 98 bis. So I hope I have answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. I should like to go back to one other aspect that was touched upon by one of my colleagues. You tell us that, for example, the charge of murder refers to several individuals, but I think that when it comes to the definition of the criminal offence of murder, if we talk about the abstract elements of the criminal offence of murder, I don't think that there is a -- that the element was that there had to be several persons murdered. When you say "several persons" in the criminal offence of murder, it is enough to have one victim to sustain this count of the indictment. So in follow-up to the question that was asked by Judge Riad, if we say that there is not enough evidence, and to a certain extent you refer yourself to the Kordic case law and you also admit, to a certain extent, that you haven't met the required standard for the charge of murder, I would like to know whether this criminal offence of murder can still stay, because it does not require several victims. The only thing that it requires is one victim. I don't know how you can respond to that. I'm talking about the abstract definition of the criminal offence of murder. What is necessary, what is required, is only one victim, not several victims. What is your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the count, at least Counts 4 and 5, but also as against the accused Zigic, Counts 6 and 7, if we look at paragraph 34, we find the universe, if you will, of victims, as well as a time frame, and it indicates a time frame between the 24th of May and the 30th of August. And then it indicates that Kvocka, Prcac, Kos, and Radic participated in the murder of prisoners, in the plural, in Omarska camp including those listed in the schedules. So those listed in the schedules are among the universe of victims. The same thing would be true in Counts 6 and 7, at paragraph 37. The same time frame is alleged, and it accuses Zigic, either alone or with others, of entering the Omarska and Keraterm camps and participating in the murder of prisoners. And then in that, proceeds to list A through D in terms of victims. So in regard to how it was charged, it was charged as murder of more than one person. Your Honours, we suggest, at the conclusion of these proceedings, you could find the accused guilty of Count 4 and 5 by what, in my practice, we would have called "by exceptions" in that you could find that the accused are guilty of murder but the exception would be you would only find murder of one victim. So that as to prove a murder charge, even if it is a cumulative charge, you have to meet all of the elements for murder, so that you have to prove that either named or unnamed persons were killed and that the accused, somehow his acts or omissions could be legally characterised in a way that would give him criminal responsibility for those murders, and that the requisite intention was present. So you could find him guilty of just one person, but it would not transform each individual victim into a separate murder count, and that is the basis for our argument: to say that you would not have a basis in the Rule to acquit for specific victims because there are no individual murder counts for each specific victim. The schedules do not give individual murder counts. They are further particulars to support the existing counts which are counts of multiple murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you very much. I don't think we have any additional questions for the parties. So this actually concludes our hearing of the arguments in support of the motion for judgement of acquittal. We will now proceed with the Status Conference, which was announced in our Scheduling Order, and we will follow the agenda indicated therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be followed by a Status Conference

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has used 53 days of hearing in order to present its evidence against the five accused in this case. In principle, the Defence has the right to use the same amount of days in order to present its case. The Chamber believes that each of the accused should have at least two weeks for the presentation of his defence. In view of that, I should like to hear the views and positions of Defence counsel, in particular, regarding the number of witnesses that they intend to call to testify at trial. However, before I give the floor to Defence counsel, I should like to mention that, as you know, we have just discussed this motion for judgement of acquittal, and the Chamber, of course, has not made a ruling as yet. What we know at this point is that the Defence is going to continue with its case. There is at least one accused who hasn't filed a motion for judgement of acquittal. And also in respect of those accused who have admitted, to a certain extent, that there are still elements that need to be discussed. So we will continue our discussions in light of that. If we take the worst case scenario, then I should like to ask each of the Defence counsel to tell us what will be the number of their witnesses in accordance with their estimate at the moment. So having said that, I will now give the floor to Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The issue that is going to be discussed during this Status Conference is linked, I must say, to our previous discussion both as regards the Defence counsel, the Prosecution, and the Chamber. From the very beginning, we have a problem involving the indictment; that is to say, the indictment that we have in this case, it's different from all other indictments before this Tribunal. You remember when I told Mr. Niemann that I hoped that he would not have me arrested, and today I have just received a confirmation of a theory from Ms. Hollis in accordance with which the Common Purpose Doctrine equals the common responsibility -- collective responsibility. Talking about an individual that have a certain position, that makes the position of the Defence very complex, because we do not know how to organise our defence. Rule 98 bis has another provision whereby the Trial Chamber may order the entry of judgement of acquittal and motion of an accused or proprio motu. In view of the allegations made by Ms. Hollis, and in view of the evidence that has been presented in this case so far, I must say that not a single witness mentioned the fact that Mr. Kvocka was present at any single murder, any single incident, any single torture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent that Defence counsel is arguing Rule 98 bis, the Prosecution objects to it. He did not submit a pleading, he has not put anyone on notice that he wishes to argue it, and we believe that given those circumstances, it is inappropriate for this counsel now to argue Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. I was wondering what your objective was, because my question concerned the presentation of your evidence, that is, the Defence case, in particular, the number of witnesses. I can understand your wish to state once again that you are in a very difficult position to organise your defence, but I don't think that it is necessary and wise to reopen the discussion that we had on a number of occasions. We are now beginning a new phase in these proceedings, and I should like your specific answer to my specific question, that is, the number of witnesses that you intend to call in support of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I do accept your criticism, but I was about to finish. I just wanted to say that the issue discussed so far has brought us into a situation where we have to do the job of the Prosecutor. And when I say that -- having said that, I can also indicate that we intend to call 27 witnesses, and we have six alternative witnesses and two affidavit witnesses, plus two expert witnesses who are supposed to give evidence. And I wanted to say -- I was about to say, that because of a certain approach, we have been brought into a position where we are held responsible for a wider area of Prijedor. The Defence was supposed to call evidence regarding the organisation of the camp, and the Prosecution has provided us with a number of materials from which it was clear that they were able to discuss the organisation of the camp itself. But it seems that we have to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, if you wish to discuss these issues, you have to file the adequate motion, the motion for the judgement of acquittal. We are now discussing the presentation of the Defence case. Okay. You have told us that you intend to call 27 witnesses, two expert witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please try to focus yourself on these specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-one affidavit witnesses, and we also intend to call a representative of the OTP to challenge the identification. The minimum amount of time that we need is two to three weeks, but it will, of course, depend on the written of -- hearing of witnesses. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. I believe that you have the order of the Chamber, issued on the 23rd of November. In that order, we indicated what would be the agenda for today, under number 2, Status Conference, the same date, in order to be able to address the following issues. And then we have the issues enumerated one by one, and we are going to follow this agenda. We work with five Defence teams and we have to be able to organise ourselves properly. Now we are discussing the number of witnesses the Defence of each accused intends to call. Afterwards we are going to take up one by one all of the issues that are contained in the agenda. Mr. Nikolic, could you tell us the number of witnesses that you intend to call in support of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The number will require a brief introduction. May it please the Court? Can I go ahead with that before I state the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But are we going to arrive at numbers that you don't know now, or have you got the number of witnesses already before you go into your introduction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be more specific, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But quickly, please, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to this question, I shall refer to Rule 82 which speaks about joint and separate trials, Rule 82 of the Rules of Procedure. Now, the number of witnesses will depend on a ruling by the Trial Chamber with respect to the pleading as regards Rule 98 bis, which was filed on the 6th of October by the Defence, and the presentation of the case for the accused Kvocka, who is before the accused Kos. And that is why it states that we feel that we will need five to seven days, but we should like to ask that Rule 82 be respected, of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Nikolic. Let us go on with the other points at a different point. Mr. Fila, you have two or three -- the right to two or three words by way of introduction, and after that I want to hear the number of witnesses you intend to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything is very simple. Are there or are there not depositions in Banja Luka? If depositions in Banja Luka exist, then I will need two weeks here. That will be sufficient. That will make 19 witnesses, three or four expert witnesses, depending, and several affidavits, which are not going to take up any time. If depositions in Banja Luka exist, then I will have 48 witnesses plus four expert witnesses, and then I will need seven days at trial here. That is the response by the Defence with respect to that issue, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stojanovic is next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I won't be trying your patience with some of the problems that we have at this point. Let me just give you a provisional piece of information. We filed a more detailed report yesterday. We intend to have 22 witnesses, three depositions, eight alternative witnesses, and three expert witnesses. I don't think I have understood what you mean by two weeks. Does that mean two times five working days? Is that what you mean by two weeks? But at all events, it is our position that we would require more time, all the more so as the accused is the only accused for three camps. I know how much time we spent with Omarska, but with Mr. Zigic, we must focus on Keraterm and Trnopolje, and this will require much greater time. So our examination of these witnesses will require longer time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic has the floor next.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Prcac plans to call to The Hague, to the Tribunal, 14 to 16 witnesses; one expert witness amongst them, and 16 affidavits. So that is the general framework for the numbers, and I think that we will be able to get through them in 14 days, in two weeks. If there are depositions in Banja Luka, however, and if the facts that we discussed previously in keeping with Rule 98 bis, then we could reduce the number of witnesses, and that will require half the amount of time than we would need otherwise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovan Simic. With respect to the number of witnesses, and we have already considered this point, they are provisional, but we are getting to know the general dimensions of the Defence case, although the numbers are provisional. So before discussing what will be presented by the Defence, we will have to discuss these points, but we have to have a general idea of what is going to happen. utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence does not intend to avail themselves of the use of protective measures except for one case which I wish to explain to you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Krstan Simic. Thank you very much. Mr. Nikolic is next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, looking at it from this perspective, we might have to request protective measures for one particular witness, but that, again, will depend upon the number of witnesses when we come down to the specifics. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you, Counsel Nikolic. Counsel Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, unfortunately, I'm going to give you the same answer. If depositions in Banja Luka exist, then protective measures, as I wrote in my submission of the 14th of December, 1999 - you have all the facts there in writing - then they will be seeking measures to travel to The Hague and to come back and safe conduct. If there are no depositions, and I will reduce the number of people from 48 to 19, as I have said, they will ask for the same measures when they come here. And those who were coming here anyway, that is to say, even if there are or there are not depositions, are not seeking protective measures. So everything is linked to Banja Luka. I apologise, but that's how things stand at the moment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we shall see what happens in Banja Luka. We are going to discuss that point later on. Perhaps this was not a convenient order for you, but we'll see to that later on. Mr. Stojanovic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In our submission, and I handed it in yesterday, we are categorical on only one case, that we will truly need protective measures, all available protective measures, for just one witness. For the moment, we don't see that we shall be needing these measures for other witnesses, but we will see what happens as time goes on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the moment, the Defence of Mr. Prcac will not be seeking any protective measures for any of the witnesses, whether they are here or in Banja Luka, depositions in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. Another question that we must consider, and I apologise to keep having to get you up on your feet, but I think a little exercise is rather welcome, is it not? The other point is the summaries of the facts on which each witness will testify. That is the second point. Article 60 ter (G) requires that summaries of the facts be supplied on which each witness will testify, and this will allow us to rationalise the presentation of evidence. And the Chamber hopes that the witnesses called to testify will not be testifying about facts that have not been contested or are under judicial inquiry. I think that the Defence might also bring in common witnesses to testify if it is a crime that all of the accused have been charged with. So with respect to the Defence case, we must bear in mind that the Prosecution -- that the Prosecutor will have to be prepared for the cross-examination. So the Prosecution will have to have information as to the events or facts on which each witness will testify. Bearing that in mind, I am now going to give the floor to Mr. Krstan Simic, once again, with respect to the summary of the facts, summaries of the facts. Where do you stand with respect to that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, up until the 15th, which is the deadline, we will -- our submission will contain all the summaries, and we shall be complying with the deadline as you have prescribed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Nikolic, may we hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will certainly be handing in summaries to the opposite side before the presentation of the case. That is what I would like to request before the Defence case of Mr. Kos proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a question to deal with here, and the question is the following: Is it a fair trial if the Defence of all five accused puts forward, on the 15th, a summary of its defence although the witness will be brought to testify in three or four months' time? Or are we supposed to present the summaries before each of us begins our case? I hope I have been clear. So either all five of us at the same time, which is not something which we find agreeable, that is, when Mr. Krstan Simic finishes, then Mr. Nikolic can go ahead; once Mr. Nikolic completes, then it is me; and when I am over, then it is Zigic. And in that sense, I would like to hear a ruling by you, and we shall respect that ruling, whatever it might be. Thank you, Your Honours. So do you want me to do it by the 15th? If you do, I will do so. But if not, then I would rather, I would prefer, the other option, because then we will see what has been proved while the counsel before me has presented the evidence. And then the Prosecution will, of course, receive summaries within eight to ten days prior to the presentation.
