utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. We should perhaps hear the response of the Prosecution, first of all, concerning what has been exposed so far. However, my idea was that the order of the presentation of evidence during the Defence case will be in accordance with the order of the indictment, that is, what we are actually doing right now. First we will hear the defence of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, Zigic, and then Prcac at the end, that is, in accordance with the order of the indictment. Each Defence team will present its defence in accordance with that order. I will give the floor to Ms. Hollis for all of the issues that have been brought up so far, or if she wants to, she can address them one by one. It's really up to you, Ms. Hollis. I don't know in what manner you wish to respond to the submissions made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding all of the submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Ms. Hollis. If you can just tell us now whether you prefer to respond to all of the questions that have been raised by the Defence or if you prefer to intervene after each issue has been brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a response for most of the questions because we believe it is between you and the Defence. There's only one issue that we would like to speak to, and that is when the accused must provide you with summaries. May we speak to that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I think it will assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we don't believe it would be a violation of a fair trial to have all of the accused submit their summaries on the 15th of December. We also believe that that would facilitate a smoother functioning of the trial as it proceeds for this reason: There is a difference in the Rules between the disclosure that is provided by the Prosecution and disclosure that is required to be provided by the Defence. There is no provision in the Rules themselves or in the Statute except in the case of notice of affirmative defences which requires disclosure by the Defence to the Prosecution of witness statements or what witnesses will testify about, except for Rule 65 ter. So if we look at the situation, the Prosecution must provide all witness statements to the Defence, and then they also must provide 65 ter which gives summaries. The only vehicle in the Rules by which the Prosecution learns the substance of the testimony of witnesses is through the vehicle of 65 ter. We suggest that in order to enable us to proceed with an effective and prepared cross-examination, that we must be provided with those summaries well in advance of the testimony. We suggest that it is not enough for the Prosecution to be given summaries eight to ten days before a case from a particular accused begins if the summaries are the only information we have about what all of those witnesses will testify to. It simply does not give us enough time to prepare effective and appropriate cross-examination. That is different than the situation that the accused are in because of the difference in the disclosure rules. So we would ask that you ask the Defence to present their summaries to you on the 15th of December, and we would also ask that those summaries be detailed enough to enable us to effectively cross-examine the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question for you. Your position is different from the Defence, but the Defence has a little bit of an additional obstacle. The Prosecution knows theoretically, and I'm sure practically, what its case will be before it goes to trial. Pretty much it knows where its witnesses are. The Defence are five different defendants, and it may be that the -- you know, some witnesses of Kvocka will say something that the Kos or the somebody else that could have an implication for them that they hadn't expected. It seems to me that you might adhere to your Rule, but there would have to be some flexibility; in other words, they would have to be at least allowed to expand if something came up in the trial that they had no reason to anticipate and their witness could take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly agree with that, and we believe that Rule applies to the Prosecution as well, because in the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence, issues may arise or questions may be resolved. We think the Rules allow for additional witnesses to be added just by the language of the Rules. When they talk about disclosure of all witness statements, the witnesses you've identified, and then if you later identify them, you have to disclose those statements as well. So we believe there is flexibility there, and we would certainly agree that witnesses can be added or taken off the list depending on how the case evolves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Pause. I was also referring to a particular witness. Say, Witness A, you find out on December 15th that Witness A is Mr. Kos' witness, and he says that when he's going to testify about 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and then during the prior presentations, Kvocka or something, some evidence comes up that now makes it necessary for Mr. Kos to cover some other aspect that this witness could cover. I just say -- I would hate to have the Prosecution leaping up and saying, "We object to their going outside of the summary because they didn't give it to us on the 19th." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we wouldn't do that, and I think our position would be that we may need a little bit of time to cross-examine on things that were caught by surprise. But our position all along is that these things happen, and there has to be flexibility to allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Fila has raised the issue of the filing of summaries of facts, and he said that he will abide by the decision of the Chamber. But I think that we can still hear and have an idea about the opinion of the Defence counsel, and to see what they think about this issue. The issue, I think, can be considered at the end. We have a list of items on our agenda, and I think that Mr. Stojanovic was about to state his position about the summaries of the facts on which each witness will testify. I hope that you have something to tell us in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the filing that I mentioned that was sent the day before yesterday, when talking about witnesses, we provided information also as to the facts on which each witness will testify. I don't know whether the Prosecutor will deem it sufficient. If they should request additional information to that effect, I believe that we will be in a position to give them that additional information only at the beginning of the presentation of our case, that is, the case for Mr. Zigic. I don't think that we will be able to provide any additional information by the 15th of December, in view of the circumstances, including the change in composition of the Defence team, and also including the situation of witnesses and other accused and their cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the position of the Defence of Mr. Prcac is identical as the position expressed by Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Fila. We also believe that it would be fair and correct for all our material to be handed over right at the beginning -- before the beginning of our case. But let me mention one other thing. The Chamber is familiar with the fact that the Defence accepted to proceed with the trial only 45 days after the arrest of the accused Prcac, so we only had 45 days in order to prepare ourselves. We have been working on the case for the Prosecution so far, and only recently have we begun to work on our case. I really think that it would be only fair for this Defence team to be allowed an additional amount of time for the filing of these summaries, and not by the 15th of December. Let me stress two other aspects. We received summaries from the Prosecution on the day of the hearing, not perhaps every time but very often, and let me mention once again the case of Witness K, in which we didn't receive anything, and that evidence was also accepted despite that fact. I think that we should stick to your order which stated that such summaries should be handed over within seven days prior to the testimony of the witness in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right, Mr. Simic. We do intend to adopt the same conditions of work for the Defence as well. So the same procedure which was used during the Prosecution case will be applied for the Defence case. That is a minimal request, I should say. If what Mr. Jovan Simic is saying is true, we must admit that the Defence has received a number of materials which enable them to cross-examine their witnesses. But the Prosecutor hasn't received anything so far except for several pieces of information. We have to continue in that perspective. The Chamber will have to make appropriate rulings because the Prosecutor must respond to the pre-trial brief of each Defence team, and the Prosecutor has the right to say, "Well, the summaries won't do. They're insufficient and we need more information." You will all remember that we spent quite some time during the Prosecution case discussing details of witness statements, several witness statements, including those given to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and statements given to the OTP for one and the same witness. You will remember that at one point in time I said that the Defence will also be required to supply detailed information to the Prosecutor; otherwise, we will not have the equality of arms that needs to be applied. We have to put something in writing; that is, the Defence must submit written filings to that effect, and then we will hear the response of the Prosecutor. But let us continue with the agenda. We have covered the issue of summaries. As regards the issue of witnesses, I think that we need to stress that such summaries should indicate the points in the indictment to which each witness will testify. This is provided for in our Rules. So when the Defence -- when filing its summaries, the Defence should also indicate which are the points in the indictment or, rather, the counts in the indictment as to which each witness will testify. I think we have already discussed the issue of the estimated length of time required for each witness, because you have already touched on this issue, and I hope that you will also indicate it in your written brief. Let us now move to the issue which might affect our work during the presentation of evidence for the Defence, that is, the issue of deposition testimony, involving the issue of the Presiding Officer, the number of witnesses that can be heard by way of deposition, whether the deposition-taking will take place here in The Hague, in Banja Luka, or some other location. Let us hear you on the issue of depositions, and if you can also tell us how many witnesses you intend to have heard by way of deposition, where do you think they should be heard, here at the seat of the Tribunal or away from the seat of the Tribunal; and how do you think we should proceed. And I should like to hear you in general terms, each of you, regarding the issue of depositions. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Kvocka supported depositions at one point for the reason that we were in a position to have to wait for the trial to begin. But as the trial has already begun and is under way, we shall not have any deposition witnesses because we should like to present the evidence before this Trial Chamber which we consider to be relevant for bringing in the right judgement. And so I don't think I need to comment further on issues which do not concern me as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, may we have your views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence was in favour of depositions while the case was in Trial Chamber III and the list of witnesses was handed in that it thought to hear through deposition. There were 12 witnesses in all of this type. In the meantime, we have given up having one witness present testimony by means of deposition, and this leaves us with 11, and that number, 11, will depend on the decision taken by the Trial Chamber with respect to Rule 98 bis, and with respect to the Kvocka case. But it principally depends on the place in which the depositions would be taken. The Defence at this point in time does not know where this would take place. The Defence preferred Banja Luka from the very beginning, and we had an agreement with the witnesses and depositions were taken and sent to the opposite side, and we told the witnesses that the depositions would take place in Banja Luka, so we're still in favour of that. The only thing that I can say with certainty is that if there were depositions in Banja Luka, the number of witnesses would quite certainly be fewer than 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila, I think that you have already spoken on the issue, but please go ahead. You have some more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I should like to say that the Defence has sent 90 per cent of the testimony of witnesses to the Prosecution and the Court at the very beginning of trial, and the witnesses -- what the witnesses will be testifying about is in the Registry and with the Prosecution, just a few of them that we haven't received yet. If the depositions are taken in Banja Luka, then, in that case, the Defence will bring three witnesses and four expert witnesses to testify before this Tribunal. Everything else will take place in Banja Luka where it is cheaper and where we'll be able to get through the job quicker. If depositions are taken in The Hague, then there's no difference. It would be just as if we had brought the witnesses to the Trial Chamber, the only difference being that the Trial Chamber can do some other work, but then that would be 19, as we said, to begin with. So that's what I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic is next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We also have a witness whose testimony would be made via deposition. We have three witnesses of this kind, that is to say, but we think that the number will be greater. And we hope that the depositions will be taken in Banja Luka, although I don't wish to present arguments in favour of that. I think they are fairly strong arguments, but we'll say more about this at a later date. So it is our position that we have testimony by deposition in Banja Luka. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point, the Defence of Mr. Prcac has envisaged just one witness to testify by deposition, and in our talk with him he insisted that he come to The Hague, that he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if we decide that the depositions are going to be in Banja Luka, then the Defence could reduce the number of witnesses and the number of days needed for trial in The Hague. And this would reduce -- as I say, reduce the number of days necessary in The Hague by half. This would, however, increase the number of deposition witnesses, but we would save time at trial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovan Simic. I think that this question of depositions was considered beforehand, and our orientation was that we could have a Presiding Officer, and all the other necessary staff that are required to undertake this task, to have them travel for one week and only one week. For security reasons, that would be the time allotted. But now I think that we should look at this issue again with a view to implementing it. The Chamber is sitting in complete form, and you have furnished us with all the necessary elements, and the Chamber will make a ruling, that is to say, to appoint a Presiding Officer. And afterwards, the entire question, as you have heard with respect to the other Chamber that tried to organise the taking of depositions, the Presiding Officer will have contacts and meetings with the parties in order to organise everything required for these depositions. And therefore we must bear in mind the conditions; that is to say, we would have just one week and see how many people we would need to get the job done, and this is something that the Chamber will see who the Presiding -- which Presiding Officer to appoint. So we have received all the necessary information from you, you have communicated it to us, and we shall make a decision on the issue. Let us now move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make a few brief comments regarding the depositions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would note, first of all, very basically, that of course Rule 90 says that, in principle, witnesses will be heard directly by the Chambers. And then Rule 71 says where it is in the interests of justice to do so, you may order depositions. Our position on this is that we support the request for depositions however long that may take if the Defence can show that the witnesses would not appear or that it is otherwise in the interests of justice for the evidence to be taken by way of deposition. It could be, Your Honours, that they would be able to make a showing that would extend beyond one week. If they were to make that, the Prosecution's position would be that Your Honours should seriously consider that and perhaps allow for more than one week. But before you get to depositions, we would suggest the following: Number 1, the Defence counsel should indicate what is the interest of justice for each of these witnesses that requires a deposition versus live testimony. And quite honestly, Your Honours, if a witness is prepared to come here to The Hague, why don't they testify live? Secondly, if they are able to show that a witness would not come to The Hague, for example, as some of them apparently would not, we would suggest Your Honours consider the alternative of videolink testimony, because that is live testimony for all practical purposes. You are seeing it as it happens; you are able to ask questions. It has worked successfully in the past. So we would suggest perhaps, as you say, you are reflecting on this issue again, that you reflect on it all the way from the beginning what has been shown in regards to the interests of justice that require it, would videolink be possible as a preferred option to live testimony? But, finally, if you are persuaded that depositions are necessary in the interest of justice, we would ask that Your Honours rule that these depositions will be conducted even if they would extend to beyond one week. And we again support the request of the Defence that should there be depositions or should there be videolink testimony, that it occur in Banja Luka. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. Are you speaking on behalf of all the counsel or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, let's wind the film back. We don't mind if it is videolink in Banja Luka or deposition in front of a Presiding Officer or testimony in front of a Presiding Officer, and generally it is out of fear that the witnesses don't want to come to The Hague. But, as we say, all of this would, I think, facilitate the Trial Chamber to come to the right decision. I accept everything that Ms. Hollis has said, especially when she said that more than one week should be allowed; even two or three weeks, because it would be a great saving for the Tribunal. Their coming and going does not cost anything. The expenditure would be zero, and it would be faster. Videolink is an expensive procedure, a costly procedure, I have seen, and this would be simpler. But, of course, the Defence will abide by any ruling that the Trial Chamber may take. Let me also mention one more detail. An alternative to all of this is an affidavit, but you don't see the person, the live person, with an affidavit, and that is the drawback there. It is just a statement, regardless of whether it is under oath or a solemn declaration or whatever you'd like to call it. It's the same thing. You don't see the actual human being, and that is the reason why I would prefer to see depositions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that the objective of deposition evidence is to speed the trial up, and we have this problem of judicial economy in this and every other case. Everything that can be done outside the courtroom should be done outside the courtroom. The witnesses who will come to The Hague to testify before the Chamber are the ones who will be testifying about the facts concerning the accused. Everything else, political, military, ethnic background, personality traits, elements that go to the sentencing, so on and so forth, including general allegations that are often of a repetitive nature, that has to be heard by other means. It is true that the principle is that of viva voce testimony; however, we have certain constraints and we have to find ways to solve this problem. There are legal systems where evidence is presented mainly in a written manner. So we should hear witnesses viva voce when they testify about facts, and as regards other matters, we have to have recourse to other means. We appreciate the contribution that you have just given us, but we have to bear in mind the principle of equality of arms when it comes to the presentation of evidence as well, and this is something that is very important for the Chamber. All those elements will be present in the decision of the Chamber. Thank you very much for the time being, Mr. Fila. I think that we have a number of other issues that need to be discussed. We have touched upon, more or less, all of the aspects having to do with the presentation of evidence and calling of witnesses. However, I think that we have skipped -- that we haven't covered the number of exhibits. Some Defence counsel have already submitted their lists of exhibits, but we need to put them in proper context. Those lists arrived at a certain point in time, and an indication was made that they were of a provisional nature. Now we have to have final lists, and I should like to hear you on the presentation of exhibits that each counsel intends to present. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't have an opportunity to react regarding the issue of witnesses. We have a very serious problem here. We have five accused in this case. Mr. Nikolic invoked Rule 82. In view of the indictment and the form of the indictment, I should like to know what will happen. I remember the practice that was adopted in the Celebici case, but I should like to know what will happen here with the cross-examination of Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, it is one of the issues on the agenda; it's item 7 on our agenda. We haven't come to that as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but this concerns only the accused Kvocka and Radic and not other Defence witnesses. But we can, of course, discuss it in the context of item 7. Let me now go back to the issue of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Defence team has submitted a list containing some 56, 57 exhibits, and within the prescribed time limits, it will also provided the list of exhibits that it intends to use during the examination of its witnesses and the presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the position of this Defence team is as follows: We intend to present several documents and to tender them into evidence, but once again, that number will depend on your ruling and the pre-Defence brief, and also it will depend on the Defence case of the accused Kvocka. But be that as it may, the Prosecution will receive on time those documents and they will have enough time to verify their authenticity, and I don't think it will disrupt in any way the usual course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our Defence team does not have any written documentation which hasn't been used or presented so far, and I do not intend to burden you with additional written material. Everything that I had has already been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila, for this present. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, together with the list of witnesses which was submitted awhile ago, we also submitted a list of exhibits. But we are intensifying the preparatory work of our case and I don't think that I will be able to give you any more specific information at this time. I will be able to do so only before the beginning -- before the opening of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence team of Mr. Prcac will provide you with all of the documents that it has at its disposal at the moment by the 15th of December. However, we reserve our right to continue with our investigation work in the preparation of the Defence, and we might come up with some additional documents which will be presented subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We seem to be forgetting about time; we are completely immersed in our work. We have been working for one hour and twenty minutes, and I think that we should really have a break at this point in order to give an opportunity to everybody to have some rest. Let's have a half-hour break at this point, and we will continue after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Let us resume our work. We cannot work beyond 5.00. So having said that, we must try and be more concise and to the point. The question now is to know whether the parties have the intention of making opening statements. Mr. Krstan Simic, how long do you think you will need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our introduction -- I think there's something wrong with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're all equal now, I think. Are you receiving the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, we said at the beginning that we planned to bring two expert witnesses; one of those witnesses will be a witness that did the psychiatric examination and report at the request of the Court and the second expert witness will be speaking about the organisation of the police force. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Krstan Simic, but where are we agenda-wise? I think we have reached point 5, Article 84, regarding the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I wasn't getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're talking about opening statements and Rule 84. Do you intend to make an opening statement? And if so, how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do intend to make an opening statement which will last between two and three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer is yes, and it will take one hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I am not getting the interpretation. Thank you. That is a very brief answer and succinct. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like Mr. Nikolic, the same applies to us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we too intend to make an opening statement which we think will last between two and three hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are also going to have an opening statement which will not go beyond one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And now we come to the cross-examination and the mutual cross-examination of the accused Kvocka and Radic. As you know, these accused testified in their own defence at the beginning of trial. We agreed that the cross-examination of the accused will not take place before the end of the presentation of the Prosecution case. Now I have a question for the Prosecutor: When does the Prosecutor think that the cross-examination of these accused will take place?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when do we think they take place, or when would we prefer that they take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would prefer to cross-examine them at the end of their cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Defence case has been presented; is that right, Madam Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, of each accused after their case has been presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as to the counsels of Mr. Kvocka and Radic, Mr. Krstan Simic, the cross-examination for you of Mr. Kvocka, how do you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I consider that in the Kvocka case, the cross-examination should start and then the Prosecution should declare its position with respect to all these issues. I am of the same opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Another question is the following: We need to know whether the Defence counsels of Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic would like to proceed with a mutual cross-examination. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I broached the subject earlier on and I was advised to leave it until this particular point, and we discussed this issue during the break, and that is the question of cross-examination and the mutual cross-examination, that is, examination of the Defence witnesses. I start out from Rule 82, which says that each of the accused be accorded the same rights as if such accused were being tried separately. Therefore, we have a Rule which prescribes how cross-examination is to be conducted, and it provides for the fact that cross-examination be restricted to the subject of the examination, that we can discuss the credibility of the witness, and that under extraordinary circumstances, the Trial Chamber can ask the witness relevant questions about the case. This opens up a very relevant question. We have five accused. Now, what is the limit up to which we can examine those witnesses? It is our view, and I think it is the view of the rest of the Defence teams, and that is the following: It is my case, they are my witnesses, and I don't mind the Prosecution asking the witnesses about all relevant cases linked to exclusively the Kvocka case. So the witnesses brought in by Kvocka and Kos, they are not witnesses of the Prosecution so they can't ask them questions relevant to another accused. And we consider that the other Defence counsels would not have the right either to pose questions to these witnesses, because we consider it to be the Kvocka case. So it is between Kvocka and the Prosecution. If we were to adopt a different attitude, then we would bring ourselves into a position where we cannot rationalise our time. I would consider that I need two hours. If we have four people, 20 minutes each, this would lead us into a chaotic situation, and that is why I don't think that justice will be denied or hampered in any way if we proceed in that way in respect to all the accused and their witnesses. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the Trial Chamber must make a ruling in this respect; otherwise, we're going to face a problem. You know all the things that can happen, everything is possible, and that it would be best if the Trial Chamber were to make a ruling on the issue, of course after having heard from our learned colleague, and we shall abide by your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Hollis, on this point, cross-examination and mutual cross-examination of the accused Kvocka and Radic, and we know that Mr. Zigic will also testify in his own defence. But independently of that, let us have your views on the cross-examination and the mutual cross-examination. Do you have an opinion there?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, in regard to the restriction that has been put forward on the content of the cross-examination, we disagree with the characterisation of Rule 89(H) and we suggest that you look closely at (iii) subparts. They do allow the cross-examining party to go beyond the evidence in chief, and also matters affecting the credibility of the witness, and indicate that where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, then you may go into that. In regards to Kvocka and Radic, there are two grounds for doing that. One is that our allegation in part of the indictment is that they were superior to the others, so the conduct of the others would have a bearing on the criminality of these accused, both Kvocka and -- I'm sorry, I should have said Kvocka and Prcac. Secondly, going back to the theory that we discussed earlier regarding the Common Purpose Doctrine, cross-examination relating to other crimes or incidents in the camp would be relevant to the accused's liability based on that. As to Kos, Radic, and Zigic, we believe we could examine as to matters that were relevant to our case which would go beyond the direct examination. We also believe that we could examine -- because of the theory of common purpose, we could go into questions about other actions in the camp. So we don't believe that we would be restricted in content as the Defence suggests we would be. If your question goes to when in the order we would cross-examine compared to the other accused, we believe that ultimately that is a matter for Your Honours. We would request we be allowed to cross-examine after the other accused have cross-examined both the witnesses and the accused who have testified or will testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Now, with respect to the Defence counsel for Kos and Prcac, I would like to hear their views and whether these accused are going to testify on their behalf, in their own defence, or not. Mr. Nikolic, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to Rule 85(C), the defendant can testify on his own behalf, and I have in view the ruling in the Celebici case, IT-90-31, of the 4th of April, 1998, in which it is stated that the accused can choose when he wishes to testify - that is under number 1 - and 2, the accused may testify at any time in the course of his case, during the trial proceedings, and that is Article 21(4)(g) of the Statute. It is expressed there. So the Defence presented the time plan, will not overstep that, and if it decides to, it will been within that time span.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Kos is going to testify on his own behalf, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I said. I did not say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. My question -- I'm asking you now: Is he going to testify in his own defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know yet, Your Honour. At this point in time, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're reserving the right to tell us at some given point in the future; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Stojanovic, what about Mr. Zigic? Have we understood that matter? Yes, he's going to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic, what about Mr. Prcac?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we take the same position as the Kos Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should just like to respond to Ms. Hollis in one sentence. Ms. Hollis and I agree absolutely on one point: The Defence does not wish to limit the Prosecution in asking the witness relevant matters but linked to Mr. Kvocka. She can ask whatever she likes, and that is our position on this problem. Ms. Hollis and I are in agreement there. She will have no limitations and no restrictions. But the witness did not mention Zigic. He did not mention anyone else, and if we went into that, then that would extend the whole thing. So that is the point we're trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will take a decision, having been provided with arguments from the two parties. I think that we now ought to look at the calendar and scheduling. If I summarise everything that we have discussed up until now, I shall go back to Article 65 ter (G) of our Rules and you will find a synthesis. All the matters we discussed in detail are set out in Rule 65 ter; that is to say, after the close of the Prosecution case and before the commencement of the Defence case, the Pre-Trial Judge shall order the Defence to file the following: A list of witnesses the Defence intends to call and all the elements which are mentioned in (G)(i); second, a list of exhibits that Defence intends to offer in its case, stating, where possible, whether the Prosecutor has any objection as to authenticity. As you see, it is the Rule which mirrors the one that we used for the Status Conference that we had for the Prosecution case and the presentation of the Prosecution case. Now you have a synthesis of all the work that we have developed today. You have this Rule which you must bear in mind. And now as to calendar, as to the schedule, we have the basis that you gave us. The Prosecutor took 53 days to present his evidence. In principle, and I underline that word, in principle, each Defence counsel will have approximately two weeks. I say "approximately two weeks," and "in principle." Now, I should like us to be able to programme our time. You are well aware of the fashion in which the proceedings evolve. So at the beginning of the Defence case, you are going to tell us how long you will take to complete your cases, and we always said that organisation is an instrument of our work; that is to say, it is an instrument to serve us and not us to serve the instrument. So we are going to exchange views and see what we can do. The calendar is the following -- that has been proposed is the following: From the 22nd to the 25th of January; from the 5th to the 8th of February, those are the sittings; from the 12th to the 16th of February; from the 5th to the 30th of March; from the 2nd to the 13th of April; from the 23rd to the 27th of April. As you know, the 16th and the 30th of April are holidays. No audiences in the week from the 16th to the 20th of April either. After that, from the 1st to the 18th of May we shall be sitting, and we envisage to have the end of the Defence case then; from the 28th of May to the 1st of June for the rebuttal by the Prosecutor; from the 12th to the 15th of June, the redirect by the Defence, rejoinder, and one day for each member of the Defence; and from the 2nd to the 10th of July, the pleadings and closing arguments. Then we have the calendar with respect to the preliminary motions. You have the Scheduling Order already with respect to this. Preliminary motions, a filing of the pre-Defence briefs on the 15th of December, 2000, and the response of the Prosecutor on the 5th of January, 2001. Pre-Defence Conference on the 12th of January, and it will be at 10.00 a.m. and not at 16 hours as is indicated. We said 16 hours because we had another matter to attend to that day. But now that we do not have to attend to that matter on that particular day, the Pre-Defence Conference will start at 10.00. I think that it might be possible or, indeed, necessary, and if so, if it is necessary, we might have a Status Conference to discuss the pre-Defence brief and the responses by the Prosecutor perhaps in the week of the 8th -- 7th of January. The 7th of January is the Orthodox Christmas so we shall bear that in mind. So it will be the 8th or the 9th of January because the 7th of January is the Orthodox Christmas. So the Status Conference could be on the 9th or 10th of January if necessary. But we're going to go through all your documents and material again, and if we find the need for an extra Status Conference, we shall invite you to attend. If we find that we don't need a Status Conference, then we go ahead with the Pre-Defence Conference on the 12th of January, as we have already stipulated in the Scheduling Order. I, therefore, think that we have the calendar for the Defence case and for the different stages of the Defence cases. We have this schedule for preparing the Status Conference. We shall contact you if we need to. I think that that exhausts our agenda for today. Let me just ask both parties whether there is any urgent matter that they wish to discuss at this point, and I give the floor to Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, there is one matter that we would like to put on the record today. As you will recall, at the end of our case, we had marked the Exhibit 3/167A, B, and C, that is, the record of interview of the accused Prcac; A being the English version, I believe; B being the B/C/S version; and C consisting of three documents that were shown to the accused during the interview. After the conclusion of our case, counsel for accused Prcac examined that transcript and has notified us and, I believe, the Court that he has no objections as to the accuracy of the content. Therefore, Your Honours, we would move again for you to admit that exhibit into evidence, and that would be 3/167A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I thought that you were actually going to clarify the situation as regards other exhibits. Hasn't there been a motion concerning exhibits that is still pending?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We filed a motion for clarification and admission of evidence. We filed that, I believe, within a short period after the conclusion of our case in chief, and that is still pending before Your Honours. I didn't wish to appear that I was attempting to hurry Your Honours. I didn't mention that since it has already been filed and is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can make a ruling for both things at the same time. But we will hear Mr. Jovan Simic as well. I think, Mr. Simic, that you have already submitted your written motion concerning this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you are quite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right. We have informed the Prosecutor of that, and the transcript is identical with the original. We have examined it, and it is up to Your Honours to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There is one final matter for Your Honours to consider and that is: During the Prosecution case, once a witness took the oath, the Prosecution was not allowed contact with the witness, and we ask Your Honours if you intend to apply the same procedure to the Defence witnesses: Once the witness takes the oath, Defence counsel may not have contact with the witness. The further refinement of that rule would be to ask Your Honours what your position will be when it is an accused who testifies. After they take the oath, will you have the same rule or a different rule? And we certainly do not request a response from Your Honours now, but we wanted to raise that for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about my colleagues, but I will tell you my personal opinion. We will apply the same rule in respect of Defence witnesses; that is, once they have been sworn in, there will be no contact between the counsel and the witness. However, the decision also made provision for certain exceptional circumstances, and I think that we have already availed ours of such exceptional circumstances. The accused can act here in his capacity of a witness, but he's, first of all, an accused in the case and I think that that justifies the application of the provision for exceptional circumstances. I can, of course, discuss it with my colleagues and we can make the appropriate ruling later on. The accused who is testifying in his own defence is in a somewhat different capacity than the regular witness, and it is a bit difficult for the accused and the counsel not to have communication during that period of time because very often an accused testifies over a period of days. But we will take into consideration your arguments and we will make a ruling. Let us perhaps hear the Defence regarding this issue. Mr. Fila, I don't know if you are going to take the floor on behalf of your colleagues as well. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this conversation is beside the point because Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic testified almost a year ago. If we should stick to the rule strictly, then I wouldn't have had an opportunity to talk to my client during that period of time. So that situation in itself is, I think, the appropriate answer to the question, whether we like it or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question for the purposes of clarification: The 15th of December and the filing of pre-trial briefs, is that in accordance with Rule 65 ter (G)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is, names of witnesses, summaries of facts, counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, indeed. Yes, Mr. Nikolic, the pre-Defence briefs are provided for in that Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honour; However, the discussion that was held here went into a different direction. On the 22nd of January, we will begin with the Kvocka case, and the estimated time that the case will take is two weeks, that is, 14 working days. And then there is a break between the 16th of February until the 5th of March. I think that if we bear in mind, if we respect Rule 82 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I think that that should be the appropriate time for the Defence of the accused Kos to present its case, and at that moment the Rule 65 ter (G) should be triggered, because only at that point in time can that Rule be applied in a specific and concrete manner. Otherwise, if we have to file the pre-Defence brief by the 15th of December, we can only discuss the matters in abstract terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Mr. Nikolic, if I understand your argument, you are telling us that you are not in a position to file the pre-Defence brief in accordance with the provisions of the relevant Rule because the discussion at this point in time is still somewhat academic for you and abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Conditionally speaking, yes, because I don't know whether by the 15th of December I will receive the decision of the Chamber pursuant to the motion which was filed in accordance with Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is why I indicated that we might need another Status Conference before the pre-Defence Conference which will treat the elements you have invoked. If we want to be really ready to proceed with the Defence case, and perhaps we will not be ready to proceed before the end of January, I think that you should put in writing your arguments that you will have to file, the pre-Defence brief, bearing in mind the first scenario, that is, if your motion is rejected. It is possible that the Chamber makes public its ruling this week or maybe next week, and then once you receive the decision, you will revise, if necessary, your pre-Defence brief. But it is also possible that the decision is made only once you have already filed your pre-Defence brief. If that should happen, we will need another Status Conference to discuss the matters which will be pending at that time before the opening of the Defence case. We have to try and proceed as expeditiously as possible, and that is why it is necessary for you to file the pre-Defence brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is one aspect, but we also have the issue of the Kvocka case which affects the position of my client. Looking at the schedule that you have suggested, I think that the Defence of the accused Kos fits perfectly in that schedule. Our intention is not to manipulate the schedule, but we want to be given an opportunity for the accused Kos to be tried separately, pursuant to Rule 82, that is, that he should receive the same treatment as if he were being tried separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nikolic, but this concerns every single accused at this trial. This particular Rule is applicable in respect of all of the accused in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honour, when you say that the Rule is applied to all of the accused. But the provision here is made that they should be accorded the same rights as if such accused were being tried separately, and this was also debated by my colleague, Mr. Fila. We do not intend to disturb the schedule that has been suggested by you, Your Honours; we can assure you of that. Let me try and make myself clear. Once the accused Kvocka has completed its case, within the period of five days, that is, on the 16th of February until the 20th of February, the Defence of Kos will be filing its pre-Defence brief in accordance with Rule 65 ter (G), which will be almost two weeks before the beginning of his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have to take up this issue once again. I believe that we said that we would come back to this question, and we should perhaps now find out whether all of the accused will present their pre-Defence briefs at the same time or not. My understanding was that the pre-Defence briefs would be filed for all of the accused by the 15th of December, because the Scheduling Order did not concern any specific accused, it concerned all of the accused in this case, and this is what is stated in the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, indeed. That is stated in the schedule. But we wanted to present our arguments to that effect, and our arguments are based upon relevant provisions of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, including Rule 82 and Article 21 of the Statute. And we also have Rule 73 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, then Article 2 of the Statute -- I'm sorry, Rule 2 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and Rule 85(C). Those are the relevant provisions which give us the basis for our position, the position that we have taken up in respect of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're going -- you're trying to say that you're not going to file your pre-Defence brief by the 15th of December but by some other date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot tell you that I'm not going to do that. I would merely like to be given an opportunity to avail myself of the rights contained in the Rules, and for me to be able to present my pre-Defence brief once the Kvocka case has been completed. Then Mr. Fila would follow, Mr. Stojanovic, and Mr. Prcac in the end. That is our common position except for the Defence team of Mr. Kvocka, for whom this issue is irrelevant, because he is the first on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, I think we finally understand your argument. I have to apologise. There has been a misunderstanding here. But as far as I understand, the position of the Defence is the following: A pre-Defence brief will, first of all, be filed in respect of Kvocka, which will be followed by Kos, then Radic, Zigic, and Prcac. Let us discuss the issue. Why such a procedure, Mr. Nikolic? Why do you think it wouldn't be such a good idea to file all of the pre-Defence briefs at the same time? How do you think that the right of an accused to have a separate trial can be endangered by the fact that his pre-Defence brief is filed at the same time as the pre-Defence briefs in respect of all his co-accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will repeat once again what the basis of our position is, and that is Rule 82 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which discusses the issue of joint and separate trials. In our view, the Rule is perfectly clear. In joint trials, each accused shall be accorded the same rights as if such accused were being tried separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Mr. Nikolic. But how can a joint filing of the pre-Defence briefs endanger this right to separate trial? In what manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, in that case, the pre-Defence brief, if it is filed separately, can be precise, specific, and concrete, because we would have already heard the case of the accused Kvocka by that time. And the pre-Defence brief of my client would be of a better quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the reason -- is that the argument that works only in favour of your client or in favour of all other accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My colleagues are joining me in my position because their situation would also be much clearer after the presentation of the case of the accused Kvocka, then Kos, so on and so forth. They will be in a much better position once they have heard the cases of their co-accused. While the case was being heard by Trial Chamber III and when discussing the issue of depositions, we already touched upon the issue of multiple witnesses and overlapping witnesses, and I think that in proceeding in this manner, we would avoid that problem. We would hear one case, complete the case, and then we would begin with the following case. In the meantime, the Defence would act pursuant to the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G). If it proceeds in that manner, I believe, I hope, that we will be very specific in our pre-Defence briefs and we would not be speaking in abstract terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you cite us any other -- any other examples here in the Tribunal of joint trials where it's been proceeded that way, either Celebici that your co-counsel was with or perhaps some other ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Celebici case is a case in point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I was following the suggestion made by Judge Wald. Mr. O'Sullivan, could you enlighten us as to how Celebici stood on that point? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Indeed, at the time of the Celebici case, there was no Rule 65 ter, but the Tribunal, under the general powers of Rule 54, ordered that the Defence, as and when the cases began, disclosed to the Prosecution the information. I may have been a little less complete than Rule 65 ter, But by and large, what Rule 65 ter obliges. So there was no obligation on the Defence to disclose it prior to the commencement of their respective cases. So it was done in the way that we're proposing here, not all at once but at a reasonable point prior to the beginning of the next Defence case. Indeed, that's the -- if I might add, it seems that that is the structure of these Rules. It is a disclosure provision, Rule 65 ter, and the key thing is the date at which that date of disclosure is triggered. And to be fair and equal among the accused, it shouldn't happen all at the same time. So there are no discrepancies between the first, second, third, and so on down the line. So it's a case of -- that's tied, I would submit, to the presumption of innocence, burden of proof, and just the general framework of the disclosure and the timing of disclosure. It's unfair or unequal to request that all of the accused disclose at the same time. The Rules do not contemplate that. There should be a staggered date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, would you like to speak to us on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few comments. First of all, Your Honour, if you look at Rule 82, we suggest that the fundamental flaw to the arguments you have heard is that Defence counsel are somehow assuming or implying that Rule 82 requires that the 65(G) submissions be given close in time to the beginning of the Defence case. We suggest that the Rule doesn't require that, nor does a fair trial require that. So this is not a matter of treating these accused as though they were being tried separately. We suggest it is purely within the discretion of the Trial Chamber as to when they order the Rule 65(G) submissions to be given, and that if you had a case where there was only one accused and there was going to be a three- or four-month delay between the close of the Prosecution case and the opening of the Defence case for that one accused, the Chamber could order that the 65 ter (G) submissions be made within a very short time after the Prosecution case closed. So there is no requirement in the Rules or in the Statute that the Defence provide the information required under 65(G), only until its case is about to start. The Rule says sometimes after the Prosecution case closes and before its case opens; that's a broad period of time. Moving to the second point they have made, and that is somehow the submission would be better if you waited until later, we suggest that they're reading too much rigidity into 65 ter (G). They already know because they've told you how many witnesses they will call if they have to address the entire case against them. They can provide the information about those witnesses by the 15th of December. If your rulings on the motions for judgement of acquittal or if the evidence that is brought out in the other presentations by the other accused somehow changes the witnesses they need to call and witnesses drop out, they simply notify the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution that these witnesses will not be called. That is not a difficult thing to do. The thing that having them provide their submissions on one date does is that, number one, it is a, we suggest, better way to organise the trial because then the submissions are all provided on the one day, and then on the following date you have established the Prosecution has to respond to all those submissions. If we do it the other way, the Prosecution will respond to five different submissions. That can take additional time, because each time you tell them they must file their submission by a certain date, you have to give us some time to respond to that submission, so that could delay the proceedings. So we don't see that the Statute or the Rules require these single submissions just before that particular accused's case goes on. We suggest that the real question is: How would you better organise the case? And also there is as a by-product of Rule 65 ter (G), of course, there is some disclosure. We suggest that the sooner the opposing side, in this instance us, receives that disclosure, the more time that we have to prepare an effective and a focused cross-examination. If those witnesses drop out, that doesn't harm the accused if they decide not to call them. Filing submissions early doesn't preclude them from changing if circumstances require it. So we believe that it is totally within your discretion as to when you want this to be filed, and we would ask that you continue to ask them to file it on the 15th of December. There is a situation that could alter that. For example, the Defence counsel for Prcac has indicated that they really have not had the time to do it. If they can persuade Your Honours that they have not had sufficient time to be able to prepare these submissions, then that's a separate basis for giving them additional time. But that is something you would have to consider after they present to you their reasons why they haven't had sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know what the experience is with any other cases involving joint trials after 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot speak to that with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Even with a little degree of certainty?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that this procedure that is being suggested has been followed. Celebici, I understand now, it has been; but as to the other cases, I'm not aware that it has been. But I would not make a statement -- a definite statement about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, you seem to find that there is no harm in presenting -- from the side of the Defence, because they can, after all, change the number of witnesses to their advantage, I mean they can reduce it and then no harm done. But what about the opposite hypothesis: They might need more witnesses after hearing one of the other accused. They might find themselves in need of more witnesses, and in that case they would be at a disadvantage if we ask them to decide it right at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is an extremely important point, and I believe that earlier in the day at some point Judge Wald raised that as well. The Prosecution's position is that filing something under 65 ter (G) or the Prosecution's submission under 65 ter should not preclude that party from presenting evidence if they can show why a changed circumstance requires it. But this is true whether they present their 65 ter submissions immediately before their case or two months before their case, because in the middle of their own case, a witness could say something that changes the circumstances and requires them to call yet another witness. We are very caught up today with the need for speedy trials, and that is an appropriate consideration. But we stress again that a speedy trial cannot be at the expense of a fair trial or a just trial. So the Court has the power to and has in the past adapted the proceedings to the situation. If justice requires they change the order, it doesn't matter when they file their submissions, they should be allowed to do so, as should the Prosecution. So we don't see that as a detriment either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As time is passing rapidly, we have to say one thing: Ms. Hollis requests that I ask a request from you for me to change the name of the witnesses, to increase the number or to reduce the numbers, which means that that is something that is up to you, whether you allow it or not. But if we accept the other solution, then I don't have to ask for a request, and five days after Kos' case I will be able to decide which witnesses I will have without asking permission from anybody. And if we have at heart a fair trial, then why should Kvocka have the advantage; that is to say, the Prosecution can prepare for him 15 days and one year for Prcac, for example. Where is the fair play there? Thirdly, let me remind you that Mr. Radic was arrested on the basis of the testimony of one individual A, and we have received three more incriminations from the Prosecution 20 days ago. The Prosecution did not adhere to that rule of theirs to give us summaries in time. We either didn't get them at all or Mr. Saxon would supply us with the summaries in the morning, 15 minutes before the proceedings went ahead. So I would like each of us, in making a request from the other side, asking the other side to do something, should show by way of their own example what should be done. And the extended indictment was in 1995 not in the year 2000. So if that is fair, then I want that fairness to be applied to me. I want to be given five days after the Kos case to see which witnesses I am going to call and to decide, and not to ask for additional permission and understanding from Ms. Hollis. Had Ms. Hollis had understanding, then in 1995 she would have charged Mladjo Radic with everything that she did later on in September or August, or whatever month it was - it's not important - because she had it in her hands. She could have done it during disclosure, but we did not receive that. So the same that was applied to them, we request that it be applied to us; that summaries are not given 15 minutes before we go ahead with trial. I can come in the morning, like Mr. Keegan, and say, "The changes for this week are such and such. We're not going to hear one witness, we're going to hear another." And now you are asking us to do so by the 15th of December, to tell you exactly who is going to come on what day, at what time. And if that is not so, then I will ask to ask the Court's indulgence to show understanding. Why should that apply to us when it did not apply to the Prosecution? Had they set the example, I would have followed it. But you must reap as you sow, as we say in our country, and I think it applies generally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, have you got anything to add? Because it is five minutes to five o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour. In principle, this discussion is something that does not concern me, but there is something that concerns my case. Everybody is setting yardsticks. How much Kvocka does, we are going to do the same. That will be our yardstick. Whereas the schedule is done in advance. And that is why I should be given all the necessary time. Because what would happen if I am given ten days - I am speaking hypothetically - and I need 15 days perhaps? And then somebody later on within those 53 days to keep the balance, there's no need for us to do that because it was done in the Kvocka case. So the question here is the correct distribution of time, because it is the first 10 or 12 days which are set as a parameter and yardstick to what will happen later on. So we don't want it to be at our disadvantage and to the advantage of everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask Mr. Jovan Simic next. Are you ready to respond in general terms? I say "in general terms," without making any specificities, with respect to the Defence of Mr. Prcac? Can you tell us now? Are you prepared to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could give a provisional programme. We have talked to many witnesses. Some witnesses are afraid to testify because of their own environment; others are afraid because of the IPTF visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can tell us all that in the pre-trial brief defence. Can you tell us what you have and what you still need? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one moment, please, for the Judges to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber makes the following ruling: Several pre-Defence briefs, multiple pre-Defence briefs, will be submitted on the same date, that there will be a single submission, and the date will be indicated in the same decision, that is, the decision on the motion for judgement of acquittal. The pre-Defence briefs will have to be submitted ten days after the publication of the said decision. The Prosecutor will have one week to file her response, one single response to several pre-Defence briefs. That was the best solution that we could have reached. We understand that everything is somewhat unclear because we haven't yet made the decision on the motion for judgement of acquittal. So I think that the best way for all of you will be to file your pre-trial briefs ten days after the publication of the decision on the motion for judgement of acquittal, and the Prosecutor will be given another seven days to file her response. This brings us to the end of our working day today. It is almost 5.00, and I think that all of us are quite tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that we have reached the end of our hearing today. I should like to thank the parties for their availability to begin at 10.00, because we realised at one point that two hours would not be enough to discuss all of the pending issues. As soon as we learned that we had enough time to hear your case today, this other case has been cancelled, we informed you of the new schedule, and I should like to thank you once again on your availability to proceed earlier on. As far as I understand, Ms. Hollis is not going to continue working with us. Am I correct in understanding that, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would depend upon how long it takes Ms. Somers to familiarise herself with the case so that she can effectively function. If she does that before the January session, then I will not be involved. If she needs a little bit more time, then I will assist in January. So I don't know. I guess, as many other things today, if this scenario, this, and if that scenario, that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see. Let me take this opportunity to wish you a Happy Christmas to all of those who celebrate it, and also to wish you a Happy New Year, and also to wish you a happy Orthodox Christmas. We worked a lot today. Thank you for your patience, once again, and I should like to thank the interpreters who have worked hard today. We really have to wind up because I think that everybody is tired. The hearing is adjourned.
